#864. Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos, FA and coach Tony Popovic at crossroads | Joey Lynch

The most immediate question thrown up by the delay of the tournament in Saudi Arabia is what it now means for Popovic

Confirmation that the Asian Cup has been postponed until December 2027 would have caught few by surprise. But the timing of Tuesday’s announcement might have, given it came well ahead of the late November timeframe hinted at by the AFC. Yet with Houthi attacks continuing across Saudi Arabia, it felt inevitable the tournament would be deferred.

However foreseeable though, it has left the Socceroos, their coach Tony Popovic and Football Australia at a crossroads.

It is a major tournament the Socceroos harboured hopes of winning. Japan would have been considered favourites; the Samurai Blue, despite having been underachievers since winning in 2011, have earned that mantle. But, despite back-to-back quarter-final exits, Australia are also acknowledged as a continental heavyweight by their peers, coming off a World Cup in which they were one of only two Asian sides to progress to the knockout stages. And with rivals such as Qatar, South Korea and Iran all aging and/or experiencing significant upheaval, the regional picture suggested they should have challenged in January.

Popovic would have been able to take to Saudi Arabia a side brimming with young talent and boasting an enviable combination of consistent improvement and valuable World Cup experience. They would have been building on an October window in which they twice met Brazil and a pair of ideal preparatory games against the 2023 Asian Cup finalists, Qatar and Jordan, in November.

Even with fitness concerns hovering over Mohamed Touré and Jordy Bos, the talent and momentum was there for the Socceroos to win a second Asian crown.

Nonetheless, there are silver linings. The tournament may benefit from a 12-month delay, as it will feel less like a post-World Cup afterthought. The postponement could also allow the Socceroos to further evolve and become even better by Christmas next year.

Another 11 months means further development, both for the Socceroos as a collective and for individuals such as Nestory Irankunda, Paul Okon-Engstler, Alessandro Circati and Lucas Herrington. Following their recent high-profile moves to some of Europe’s biggest clubs and leagues, that progression could be significant. It also allows for injured players such as Bos, Touré and Lewis Miller time to recover, while other youngsters yet to establish themselves get more time to impress.

In this scenario, the hope is that a bird in the hand isn’t worth two in the bush – that more injuries don’t strike and that veterans such as Jackson Irvine and Aziz Behich maintain their current form.

But the more immediate question arising from the announcement is what it means for Popovic. The November window is now ostensibly the 53-year-old’s last as Socceroos coach; the contract extension he signed ahead of the World Cup, which was supposed to take him through this tournament, concludes on a definitive date rather than a nebulous “post Asian Cup” marker.

Popovic and Football Australia face a challenge neither would have expected when they hammered out – at the coach’s insistence – a deal that only took him through to the end of the continental showpiece. A similar scenario confronts Graham Arnold with Iraq, while Japan have already signalled that Hajime Moriyasu will be replaced by Go Oiwa.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

Is it now simply a matter of extending Popovic’s deal through to 21 January 2028? Given the federation offered him that longer-term deal, and executives such as Heather Garriock and Martin Kugeler have never been anything but effusive in their praise, it’s almost certain Popovic would be able to if he wants. But does he?

He would have had his reasons for not wanting to be locked into a longer-term deal. And as a football-obsessed workhorse, it’s entirely possible he’d have ambitions to return to the grind of club football. His stock is high after leading the Socceroos to the World Cup’s knockout stages, and further bolstered by a window where his side performed well against Brazil and he drew praise from Carlo Ancelotti. If he wants a new challenge, he has earned one.

But what if he stays, only to depart after another 12 months? Kevin Muscat has always appeared to be an obvious successor, especially given he’ll be a free agent after the imminent conclusion of the Chinese Super League. And if Popovic does opt to depart, he should be offered the job. But would he – or another preferred candidate – be willing to wait a year, especially with World Cup qualification will still beginning in September? Does Football Australia risk being left to scramble come 2028 if they don’t play their cards right?

Just like seemingly everything else in Australian football, the postponement of the Asian Cup presents as both a potential opportunity and a curse.

#863. 'We fell behind' - what does new San Siro deal mean for AC Milan and Inter?

Why time is running out for the iconic San Siro

When AC Milan and city rivals Inter jointly revealed the design of their planned new stadium on Thursday, one thing stood out in particular - the name.

The 71,500-seater arena the clubs aim to share from 2031 onwards, replacing the iconic San Siro, will be called the Generali Stadium.

Generali is an Italian insurance company, and the firm has agreed to pay about 650m euros (Â£542m) for naming rights through to 2052.

The length and value of the agreement makes it one of the most lucrative naming-rights deals in sports history.

Stadium naming rights are, of course, nothing new in elite football. The champions of England and Germany both play in arenas built in the 21st century that have always been known by their sponsors' name, and plenty more stadiums across the continent have been partly financed by revenue from naming rights.

But in recent years, some clubs have struggled to sell them.

It was thought that both Tottenham Hotspur and West Ham would look to sell the rights to their new stadiums' names, but as yet neither have. Liverpool aimed to sell the name of a new stand they built in 2016 but no such deal has been agreed.

So, what do these stadium plans mean for AC Milan and Inter, what underpins the viability of expensive new football grounds, and what impact do culture and history have?

AC Milan and Inter are owned by separate US-based investment firms and in the joint announcement described the Generali Stadium as "a new home for generations of supporters, and a destination designed to contribute to the cultural, economic and urban development of the city".

The demolition of San Siro has been discussed for decades, and the clubs believe its deterioration and lack of modern features are significant reasons behind their progressive fall lower down the pecking order at the top of European football.

The new stadium is expected to cost about 1.2bn euros (Â£1bn) to construct, and the clubs aim to generate income by selling just under 12,000 of the seats as premium or hospitality, and host a wider array of events like concerts and fixtures in other sports.

"This is the biggest stadium naming-rights deal in the history of global sports," AC Milan owner Gerry Cardinale told BBC Sport.

"Thatâs a significant achievement in its own right and especially in the context of having been done in Italy and what it means to bring Italy back to the world stage of football.

"But if youâre looking at this purely as an annual sponsorship payment, youâre missing the bigger picture.

"The stadium is what fundamentally transforms our economic model - matchday revenues, hospitality, premium experiences, entertainment and commercial opportunities.

"These are the things that allow us to compete with the biggest clubs in Europe."

AC Milan have played at San Siro for 100 years, while Inter moved in 1947. The two clubs paid 197m euros (Â£164m) to buy the stadium and surrounding land in 2025.

The plans for the new stadium have faced opposition from some supporters, with some Inter fans protesting outside the venue where the plans were announced by carrying a banner reading 'You will never extinguish the lights at San Siro' and chanting "Hands off San Siro".

"You cannot compete consistently with the best clubs in the world without having the infrastructure and economic model to support that ambition," added Cardinale.

"The Premier League has set the benchmark in terms of commercial development and infrastructure. Italian football has fallen behind, and we need to change that.

"This stadium is a massive step forward, not just for AC Milan but potentially for the whole of Serie A."

The Generali Stadium will be built adjacent to San Siro, which will be knocked down once construction is complete

AC Milan v Inter and the tale of an iconic image

The two decades of naming rights paid for by Generali break down to about Â£27m per season - Â£13.5m per year, per club.

New stadiums are rarely built in Italy, with many Serie A stadiums in varying states of disrepair and in need of renovation before the country jointly hosts Euro 2032 with Turkey.

That means AC Milan and Inter have focused on selling a rare proposition.

"The 20-year deal is key - having that guaranteed long-term incomes gives the clubs security," said Dan Plumley - sport finance expert at Loughborough University.

"The money stacks up pretty well. Spotify pay around 20m euros (Â£17m) to sponsor Barcelona's Camp Nou per season, so now the Milan clubs aren't too far off that figure.

"What a lot of these partners are looking for is a long-term relationship because they can build their profile as expand around the world, pushing themselves into regions like Asia and Africa, and football can be very valuable for that.

"It couldn't be done at San Siro because everybody would have just carried on calling it that. Getting in early makes the sponsor part of the new history and is a really smart play from a business point of view."

The architects behind AC Milan and Inter's planned shared stadium saying it is designed to bring fans as close to the pitch as possible

Historically, the home of stadium naming rights has been the US, where the majority of arenas in most sports are known by a sponsor name.

In European football, similar deals have been most common in Germany, where major companies have direct ownership links to some of the country's biggest clubs including Bayer Leverkusen and Wolfsburg.

"It's really difficult to do naming-rights deals in English football because of our history and culture," said Plumley.

"The clubs and potential naming partners know that fans around the world could strongly oppose a deal, because it's less common here, so the value becomes less attractive."

Timing and performance on the pitch are key considerations when clubs are planning to sell the stadium name.

"As a club you don't want to just do a cheap deal and give the name away for a few million just because it's extra revenue," said Plumley.

"Clubs like Spurs or West Ham know there is a trade-off between not just agreeing something because it's a bit of extra value, having a deal that genuinely makes a difference financially, and doing something that the fans will tolerate.

"Sometimes the balance just isn't right, and some of the most successful clubs in the world would rather hold on and protect their overall value and hold off and sell when their performance is at its peak - being in the Champions League is key to that.

"Everton weren't in a position in terms of results to go out and get a big global name paying a huge amount every year, so a more local partner [the Hill Dickinson law firm] made sense."

#862. Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear

The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.

For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.

Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon Rainforest turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.

Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the nascent carbon removal industry's ability to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals.

The UN warns any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.

"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working.

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies.

"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

#861. Kane beat Mbappe to Ballon d'Or by just 28 points

'My heart was beating so fast' - Kane wins Ballon D'or

Harry Kane beat second-placed Kylian Mbappe to the men's Ballon d'Or by just 28 points - one of the smallest winning margins in the award's history.

Organisers released voting numbers on Saturday, showing that England captain Kane was awarded 1,055 points, compared with 1,027 for Real Madrid's France forward Mbappe.

Bayern Munich striker Kane became the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001, while France talisman Mbappe also claimed his best finish, ending up well clear of Spain forward Lamine Yamal, who was third with 881 points.

It was the smallest winning margin since Argentina great Lionel Messi beat Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk by seven points in 2019, while the men's Ballon d'Or has twice been decided by a single point.

That happened when England World Cup winner Bobby Charlton, who was later knighted, beat Portugal star Eusebio by the smallest possible margin in 1966, and Germany defender Matthias Sammer repeated the tight one-point victory when he edged out Brazil striker Ronaldo in 1996.

Mbappe may take heart from Ronaldo's Ballon d'Or experience as the legendary frontman, who presented Kane with his award in London on Monday, went on to win in 1997 and again in 2002.

Harry Kane is the fifth English player to win the Ballon d'Or, after Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966), Kevin Keegan (1978 & 1979) and Michael Owen (2001)

Kane clinched the prize after scoring 73 goals in 65 matches last season, helping Bayern Munich to a league and cup double and leading England to a third-place finish at the World Cup.

The award is decided by votes from 100 journalists, using a weighted points system.

Speaking about Mbappe missing out on the award, Real Madrid head coach Jose Mourinho said the 27-year-old was dealing brilliantly with the disappointment.

"Kylian is very intelligent and mature. He has very high self-esteem. And at the same time, he has class," Mourinho said before Real's game against Racing Santander on Sunday in La Liga.

"The way he handled the Ballon d'Or for Harryâ¦ all I saw and felt was class. And respect.

"It's one thing to know you're the best, and another to have respect for someone who has also worked hard to win a trophy. All I see in him is class."

#860. KATSEYE Apologizes After Cancelling Concert 30 Minutes Before Showtime

KATSEYE apologized to fans after being forced to cancel their Detroit concert on Nov. 3 just half an hour before showtime: “We are incredibly disappointed.”

Tonight KATSEYE might need to take a break.

Fans of the girl group—consisting of members Daniela Avanzini, Yoonchae, Lara Raj and Megan Skiendiel, as well as Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza, who are currently on hiatus—were disappointed when the “Tonight I Might” group’s Nov. 3 concert in Detroit was called off just half an hour before the group was set to take the stage.

“We're so sorry to share that tonight's show at Little Caesars Arena has been postponed due to illness,” KATSEYE wrote in a statement shared to Instagram Stories. “Unfortunately, Megan is unwell and unable to perform tonight, and we want to make sure she has the time she needs to rest and recover.”

Knowing such a last-minute change could have a gnarly reaction among fans, the band also apologized to their loyal EYEKONS.

“We know so many of you have traveled, made plans, and been looking forward to tonight,” they continued. “We are incredibly disappointed that we won't get to see you, and we're truly sorry for the inconvenience.”

“Thank you for your patience, understanding, and for always showing us so much love,” they concluded. “We love you and can't wait to see you soon.”

An update from the concert’s venue, the Little Caesars Arena, expressed regret that the show had to be postponed and told fans to hold onto their tickets, as they would valid when a new date for the city was announced.

The reaction on social media was mixed, with many fans frustrated by the postponement, while others defended the KATSEYE members.

“Refund everybody the Ubers, flights, hotels they booked etc etc. This is just unacceptable,” one user commented under one of the group’s Instagram posts, while another said, “This is saddening.”

One fan, however, wrote, “Before they’re artists they’re human beings — everyone leave my girls alone. Everyone’s always saying they need a break, but when they cancel a show due to illness suddenly they’re villains? What more do you people want from them truly.”

While KATSEYE has been down two members since August, the “Gnarly” singers recently confirmed Laforteza would return in January. (Bannerman has yet to confirm her own return.)

For the rest of KATSEYE, Laforteza’s scheduled return put some wind back in their sails.

"We are so happy that she's coming back," Raj told E! News at the 2026 Victoria's Secret Fashion Show on Oct. 18. "We're so proud of her. She's really been so brave."

"We respect her so much for taking the space and taking time for her health," she continued. "She's our sister, so we can't wait for her to come back."

For more stars who, like Forteza, have been candid about prioritizing their mental health, read on.

The Grammy winner has been very open about how she protects her energy, such as ignoring haters on social media, while also sharing her advice for those who may need help.

"When people ask me what I'd say to somebody looking for advice on mental health, the only thing I can say is patience," she told Vogue. "I had patience with myself. I didn't take that last step. I waited. Things fade."

The Frozen star has talked for years about her strategies for coping with her mental health at public keynotes and even on her Instagram Stories.

She has advocated for finding the methods that help you best, which for her, according to Health, can include medication, listing ten positive things in her life for every negative thought and getting plenty of exercise.

While everyone was trying to make the best of socially distancing to slow the coronavirus pandemic, the "Firework" artist got real about how situations like this can also be extremely stressful.

"Sometimes I don't know what's worse trying to avoid the virus or the waves of depression that come with this new norm," she shared on Twitter. Katy talked about how she manages those waves, writing, "There is not really anywhere to go besides my car. So I go to my car a lot. That is my safe space."

The model, who teamed up with designer Kenneth Cole to raise awareness for The Mental Health Coalition, spoke on Good Morning America about her own experiences with anxiety.

She recalled after her panic attacks started recurring, she, "finally kind of got the information that I needed about it."

"For me, I have good days and I have some really anxious days, so I'm really off and on," Kendall expressed, adding that was why she wanted to become involved with the movement. "What I hope to accomplish is for people to not feel as alone."

The rapper (real name Radric Davis) revealed in his October 2025 book Episodes: The Diary of a Recovering Mad Man that he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which prompted a mental health episode in 2020.

“After that, I was like, ‘Man, I got to really just hold myself accountable and take care of my health,’” he said on an episode of The Breakfast Club. “I don’t never want to have an episode again. I’m gonna see a therapist, [even] if I have to take medicine.”

In addition to his hope that his vulnerability would help others in need, Gucci Mane said that his kids Ice Davis and Iceland Ka’oir Davis with wife Keyshia Ka’Oir inspired him to seek help amid his episode.

“My wife was pregnant with my little boy,” he continued. “I don’t want to raise a family and then my mental health [is] gone. What if I have an episode I can’t come back from? So, I just started doing the work and started seeking help.”

In October 2026, the daughter of Teresa Giudice and Joe Giudice shared she was getting treatment for bipolar disorder in a candid update about her mental health journey.

"I do struggle with mental health issues," Milania told followers in an Oct. 12 Instagram video. "I am bipolar. I struggle with depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD and I am not ashamed of any of my mental health disorders because I'm currently at a treatment center, my mom's on her way to come visit me today."

The then-20-year-old added that "this summer hit me like a bus" after Milania was arrested for assault in May and her best friend Victoria Zardoya died suddenly in July.

"A lot of things happened in a short amount of time and I'm trying to just process everything," the University of Tampa student noted. "It's really hard being in the public light while you go through things in life."

The Gossip Girl alum detailed his experience as a child actor with what he described as "body dysmorphia."

“I know that I hated my body,” Penn told The Guardian in April 2025, “and simply wanted a different one.”

In response to the weight he gained following his parents' divorce, he added,  “There was just a period where, coming out of depression and isolation, I was jumping wilfully into, but also being thrust into, this world where the more conventionally beautiful I seemed, the more successful I might be, the more value I might have.”

Despite the mental struggles, though, Penn credited his ability to persist to his spirituality.

“That is what allowed me to persevere through the disillusionment, all the things I’d been grappling with,” he explained, “and then come back to it all, but with hopefully some kind of inner transformation.”

The Scrubs alum has been vocal about her past difficult relationship with food.

“Some may call it an eating disorder, I just call it my life,” she said on the The Funny Thing Is podcast. “My drug of choice was always food. I did crazy s--t with it.”

She added, “I would over-exercise, and there was a sprinkle of bulimia in there.”

Though she has confessed her struggles with her diet, she has also shared her progress with her health and fitness goals.

“When I was 23, I cut all sugar out of my diet, quit drinking, and found yoga and breathing and stretching,” she told Bon Appétit in 2017. “That’s the best Ritalin you could give anyone."

She continued, "I’m an actress with food issues and body image issues—that's real. But I'm trying to heal that part of myself and also handle my physical issues naturally by putting the best things into my body."

The Full House alum reflected on her mental health journey and navigating her battle with depression.

"It's very difficult to speak out about it, even to your most trusted people," she shared on her Candace Cameron Bure Podcast. "At least for me, I feel like I should be strong enough to overcome that and then it feels so weak."

The Black Adam actor has been open about having depression and how it can be difficult for men to talk about their mental health.

"We all go thru the sludge/shit and depression never discriminates. Took me a long time to realize it but the key is to not be afraid to open up," he wrote on Twitter. "Especially us dudes have a tendency to keep it in. You're not alone."

The Duke of Sussex helped break down some of the stigma around seeking help for mental health when, in an interview with the Telegraph, he opened up about his own journey with therapy. As he told the outlet, "The experience I have had is that once you start talking about it, you realize that actually you're part of quite a big club."

Another proponent of seeking professional help, the Empire star has been open about her struggles with depression."I have a therapist that I speak to," she previously told Variety. "That's the only way I can get through it."

Taraji even started The Boris Lawrence Henson Foundation, which works to reduce the stigma around mental health in the African American community and also works to increase the number of Black therapists.

The Grammy winner explained that experiences with an eating disorder and stage freight led her to start a form of PTSD treatment called MDMA and and psilocybin therapy.

“I was touring without stage fright for the first time,” she told Rolling Stone in May 2025. “There was a hook around my guts and everyone in the room was having the same feeling, [like] there’d been a huge pressure change. It made me realize how much I love and kind of need that very deep, visceral response to feel my music.”

She added that her renewed focus on her mental health, as well as her decision to stop taking birth control, caused her understanding of her own gender to become “more expansive.”

“I felt like stopping taking my birth control, I had cut some sort of cord between myself and this regulated femininity,” she continued. “It sounds crazy, but I felt that all of a sudden, I was off the map of femininity. And I totally believed that that allowed things to open up.”

"When I was in middle school, I was struggling with severe anxiety and depression and the help and support I received from my family and a therapist saved my life," the Riverdale actress wrote on Instagram in 2017.  "Asking for help is the first step. You are more precious to this world than you'll ever know."

The “What He Didn’t Do” singer shared insight into what her life has been like during her yearslong battle with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

“I would have told you three years ago my anxiety started during my divorce in Covid,” Carly said an August 2025 episode of Bunnie Xo’s Dumb Blonde podcast. “But I’ve had crippling OCD since I was a child.”

“I got really conditioned over the last 10 years to just zip it up and deal with it, and it just kind of got to a place where a couple years ago I just had to really start back into therapy, start really, like, trying to figure out all of these different things,” she continued. “Like, recognizing OCD was something—no, that didn’t come in 2020, that’s been there since I was 6 or 7.”

While the cookbook author is the proud parent to four kiddos, she's also been open about postpartum depression that many new mothers experience but feel like they cannot talk about.

"It got easier and easier to say it aloud every time," she wrote in an open letter to Glamour in 2017. "I want people to know it can happen to anybody and I don't want people who have it to feel embarrassed or to feel alone."

While promoting her book Mirror, Mirror, the model opened up to The Edit magazine about facing depression and suicidal thoughts as a teenager, saying she felt "something dark" in her during that time.

"I relied too much on love, too much on other people to make me happy, and I needed to learn to be happy by myself," Cara told the publication, via W. "So now I can be by myself, I can be happy. It took me a long time."

The "Thank U, Next" artist has encouraged fans to seek help if they need, responding to a Twitter user who joked about wondering who Ariana's therapist is with, "lmaoaoo this is funny as f--k but in all honesty therapy has saved my life so many times."

"If you're afraid to ask for help, don't be," she continued. "u don't have to be in constant pain & u can process trauma. I've got a lot of work to do but it's a start to even be aware that it's possible."

The singer has been open about her journey with addiction, sobriety, mental health and more, including many of those aspects of her life within her music.

She also continually reminds fans that working on your mental health is an ongoing process where there will be some bad days, previously writing on Instagram, "A reminder to anyone struggling out there - this life is a journey with tons of ups and downs but you can't give up."

Not only has the actress taken on roles that deal with mental health, such as her role as Rue in the teen drama Euphoria, she's also addressed those issues in her own life, too.

Back in 2013, Zendaya wrote on her now-defunct app that she struggled with anxiety after an appearance on Ellen where her mic went out. She has since learned ways to manage those feelings, adding, "Sometimes you just have to take a step back so things stop stressin' you."

The singer candidly described her mental health journey with WSJ Magazine, saying, "My highs were really high, and my lows would take me out for weeks at a time."

"I found out I do suffer from mental health issues," she shared. "I got on the right medication, and my life has been completely changed."

The Grammy winner made it her mission to spread kindness and be open about mental health, including her own.

"I have struggled for a long time, both being public and not public about my mental health issues or my mental illness," she said during the Global Changemakers Award at Children Mending Hearts' Empathy Rocks fundraiser in 2018. "But, I truly believe that secrets keep you sick."

#859. Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames

There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe

Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.

Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.

Until United are equipped to repeat their second 45 minutes on a weekly basis, which requires systemic change in departments far outside the technical area, even if Carrick’s head will surely be first on the block, nobody is likely to deliver them from ongoing psychodrama. History may tell that his heavily maligned players were fruitlessly raging against the dying of the light in blowing Roma out of the water. But their achievement here was worth savouring for its discrete brilliance and, perhaps, the wholesome powers that ultimately wrought it.

Kobbie Mainoo had been introduced as “Manchester born and bred”, to obligatory cheers, when the teams were read out. Any emotional heartstring is worth plucking on at the moment but there was something grounding about seeing the midfielder, largely injured over the past month and an onlooker while his colleagues’ fortunes spiralled, return to the starting XI. Mainoo was far from alone in enduring a tentative, twitchy, flustered first half but was caught flat-footed when Marten de Roon mugged him near halfway, setting in train the move that exposed an execrably organised backline for Matías Soulé’s opener.

At 2-0, another crossfield ball from the left having triggered United’s defence into recidivism, Mainoo attempted to raise spirits by surging through the middle on his own and spraying the ball right under pressure. There was no more nourishing gruel on offer than this; the only nagging glimmer of possibility was that Roma, for all their broad control, did not look like the kind of side that would withstand any gale that came their way.

When Carlos Baleba, eye-catching in phases but loose in possession, pulled up with Bryan Mbeumo ready for a tap-in, the notes of misery deepened. But the subsequent introduction of Youri Tielemans, in his element against opponents whose intensity was evidently sagging, created angles and spaces that had previously seemed figments of the mind. United were fortunate when Bruno Fernandes converted his soft, twice-taken penalty; they were presented with parity when Leonardo Balerdi’s air-kick afforded Matheus Cunha a chance he could barely miss. The die, though, had long been cast through their waves of slick, insistent pressure.

So it fell for Mainoo and another academy product, Shea Lacey, to tee up the coup de grace. Lacey hails from Liverpool but there is no need to whisper that: his credentials since childhood have firmly passed muster. While Lisandro Martínez was lightly booed on to the pitch in the 75th minute, Lacey arrived with him to raptures. How poetic it was that Mainoo, speeding up an attack before quickly shifting the ball right, and the mesmerising Lacey, should complete the revival.

Lacey’s jink inside and left-footed pass whipped into Cunha were genuinely breathtaking. So was the finish and so, too, the reaction. Few do it quite like an Old Trafford crowd on a European night. This is still a citadel like no other, even if its strains nowadays alternate between dubbing Mainoo unplayable and impolitely requesting the Glazers to make haste back across the Atlantic.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The contradictions fizzed everywhere on this thick, still night. Earlier on Wednesday Carrick will doubtless have been spared the news that sacking season had already visited the Ineos football empire. At this point Jim Ratcliffe’s sporting citadels are more akin to a line of Dickensian rubbish heaps, their proprietor a modern-day golden dustman, and the plug had been pulled on Luka Elsner and United’s hapless junior sibling, Lausanne Sport. They are bottom of the Swiss top flight and results, a club statement explained, had been the determining factor in the manager’s demise.

They have not exactly helped Carrick either. Mainoo had claimed in a transactionally toned pre-match press conference that United could be “one win away” from changing the shape and scope of their season. In reality all that can be guaranteed about whatever occurs next is the sheer theatre of it. Of course it is Unai Emery, discussion whose suitability or otherwise for any United vacancy has brought surprising ramifications, who walks into this perplexing cocktail of loathing and unconditional support this weekend. Carrick will need the football to perform him a few more favours yet.

#858. Worst in the EFL - the team with a penalty problem

Shaquille Gwengwe is among several Newport players to miss from the penalty spot

While fans would normally celebrate their team earning a penalty, Newport County supporters could be forgiven for putting their heads in their hands.

With three-quarters of penalties successfully converted, on average, earning a spot kick would normally be reason to celebrate.

Not so for Newport where anticipation has been replaced by apprehension.

Across the past two seasons, they have converted just two of nine penalties in all competitions - and only one of six in League Two.

Their 16.7% conversion rate is the worst in the entire English Football League (EFL).

And for a team just two points off the play-offs, missed penalties could prove costly.

Three different managers and several players have tried to find the formula, but the outcome has remained remarkably similar.

There was hope Harrison Biggins had ended the slump when he netted from the spot in a draw at Rotherham in October.

Four days later, that optimism evaporated.

The midfielder stepped up against Cheltenham Town but, having chosen the same side, saw his effort saved in the 1-0 defeat.

Manager Hayden Mullins refused to blame Biggins after his miss at Cheltenham and, having done the job himself as a player, has sympathy.

"We never lay any blame on anyone who steps up to take a penalty," said the 47-year-old.

"Penalties are always tough. Harrison scored the game before [but] it's a game of cat and mouse really between you and the goalkeeper.

"You don't know what the goalkeeper is thinking, all you can do is pick a side and execute it with aggression."

Dibley-Dias to miss County's game against Chesterfield

Exiles' Mullins not given enough credit - Jenkins

While a player may not be able to predict a goalkeeper's thought process, recent penalties may have handed Stanway a clue.

Six of Newport's last nine penalties have been aimed to the right and - on each occasion - the keeper has guessed correctly with Cameron Antwi, Nathaniel Opoku, Bobby Kamwa and Shaquille Gwengwe all denied. Only Biggins' effort at Rotherham found the net.

Even when Newport altered their approach, the result was often no different.

Ged Garner was denied to the left against Swindon Town and Yahya Bamba - aiming for the top corner - saw his effort ruled out for a double touch.

Bamba converted the retake by waiting for the goalkeeper to move, a method similar to manager Mullins' own approach during his midfield days with Crystal Palace, West Ham and Portsmouth.

"I know how hard it is. Everyone's got their own technique," said Mullins.

"I would run up, have one eye on the goalkeeper and whichever way he went, I would go the other way, but it's brave."

Newport County have the worst conversion rate from the spot in the entire EFL

It begs the question whether or not Newport practice penalties.

They have not always struggled from the spot and between 2023 and 2025, scored 10 of 13 between forwards Will Evans and Omar Bogle.

Mullins prefers to hand sole responsibility to to his centre-forward but has been without Shaquille Gwenge through suspension for the past three games - during which Newport have missed two penalties - since missing from the spot himself.

Gwenge is available again and Mullins insisted the striker - with six goals already this season - practices penalties "for a long time" after training.

But the County boss says he would "never spend too much energy" worrying about the miserable success rate.

"Penalties are down to a lot of things - fatigue, mindset, where you are, who you're taking it in front of, how you feel at that time and who you're up against," he said.

"We can look at it and practice as much as we can.

"We'll be ready for the next time we take it and hopefully it goes our way."

#857. Matthew McConaughey’s Family Photos Are Alright, Alright, Alright

Matthew McConaughey doesn't want to lose a minute of quality time with wife Camila Alves McConaughey and kids Levi, Vida and Livingston. See the How to Lose a Guy in 10 Day star's family photos.

Matthew McConaughey’s latest milestone took way more than 10 days.

The How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days star turns 57 years old Nov. 4. And unlike that love fern, he’s continuing to grow.

Though, Matthew admits his excitement for his sixth decade didn’t sprout right away.

"The first few years of 50s were a little wobbly for me," he noted on Jay Shetty’s On Purpose podcast in January. "So you go, ‘Oh, is this that midlife crisis?'"Actually, the Oscar winner prefers a different term."Sounds like a midlife, for a lack of a better word, opportunity," he continued. "It’s a time where, for whatever reason, man looks back and goes, ‘What have I done, and now where am I going?'"

It’s a journey that’s made Matthew focus more on his own story versus the ones he tells on the big screen."The challenge that keeps just gnawing at me since I’ve turned 50 is, 'What’s your documentary?'" he explained. “Are you a character in life, in the big show—the one that 'action' was called the day you were born and 'cut' will be called the day you die?"

And as the Interstellar alum begins his next act, he’s grateful to be surrounded by his cast of family members, including wife Camila Alves McConaughey and their kids Levi, 18, Vida, 16, and Livingston, 13.

“As life gets big—you’ve got a career and you’ve got a family—there’s many parts to play: Father, husband, performer, writer, whatever those are," Matthew added. "Instead of feeling like five different hats you gotta wear one day, you go, 'Oh, that’s all part of the same story. That’s all part of the same man I am.'"

One who’s proud to be a part of the dad club.

"The only thing I ever knew I wanted to be was a father," the Dallas Buyers Club star told People in 2020. "And it's remained the pinnacle for me. Being a dad was always my only dream…I can't think of anything being more important."

And if scrolling through Matthew’s family photos sounds alright, alright, alright to you, read on.

Levi and his sister Vida joined their parents at the premiere of their dad's series Brothers.

The Oscar winner, his wife and their three kids coordinated outfits while attending the Mack, Jack & McConaughey Gala together in Austin, Texas in April 2025.

Camila and Livingston checked out the solar exclipse in April 2024.

Levi shared this family photo in honor of his dad's birthday 54th birthday in 2023, writing on Instagram, "People know Matthew Mcconaughey as an Actor and now a writer, but I know him as my father."

Matthew and Livingston met Golden State Warriors star Draymond Green in November 2023.

This family time at Paris Fashion Week was magnifique!

"Surf souvenirs," Matthew captioned this March 2023 pic of son Levi.

The How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days alum gave Livingston a haircut as Levi looked on in February 2023.

"Uncle @woodyharrelson is questioning if the cake is vegan or not!!!" Camila wrote on Instagram in January 2023 for her and Matthew's daughter Vida's 13th birthday. "How does this go people! Time flies… 13! You are my ray of sunshine Vida!!!"

In December 2022, Camila wrote, "We get the trailer they are responsible for the tent… #ontheroad."

#856. Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Bart Verbruggen (Brighton): He was unreal. Lots of saves which kept Brighton in it at Manchester City, even the last-ditch stop where it hit him in the face.

Just an impenetrable wall. Brighton should really have lost by two or three goals, but Verbruggen was the reason they managed to hold on for a 1-0 win.

Archie Gray (Tottenham): I'm going with a fully north London back four. Gray scored and defended really well against Crystal Palace. He was under a lot of pressure when Tottenham were in bad form and got a lot of stick, but now Spurs are starting to pick up I'm going to give him a bit of credit.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): He was a beast in Arsenal's 1-0 win at Anfield. Head it, kick it, throw your body in front of the ball. He defended and fought for the team, getting the job done.

Jan Paul van Hecke (Tottenham): Van Hecke got a goal and he's really growing into his role at Spurs. I still think he was a little bit overpriced, but all in all he's had a solid start, coming up with a few goals. Micky van de Ven next to him gives him confidence that he can go and be really aggressive, because Van der Ven will cover him with his pace.

Jurrien Timber (Arsenal): Timber got away with a shirt pull on Alexander Isak and I'm really surprised the referee and video assistant referee (VAR) didn't look at it. But I thought he recovered and defended really well at full-back.

Romeo Lavia (Chelsea): I thought Lavia was excellent for Chelsea. People will turn to Manchester United having 10 men, but the 60 minutes before that Chelsea were all over the place. Lavia was the only constant breaking up play, keeping the ball moving. Plus he had an assist.

Declan Rice (Arsenal): A proper captain's performance, he gets the job done all over the pitch. He got a little assist for himself, too.

Tatsuhiro Sakamoto (Coventry): Sakamoto goes unnoticed by a lot of people, but I think he works really hard for the team and he is very humble in his approach. On Saturday he also delivered in a massive win for his team against Sunderland.

Johan Manzambi (Aston Villa): Another assist for the 21-year-old who is just flying. His confidence is through the roof and he is taking over this Villa team. Really good player, only going to get better. He was taken off thinking about the Champions League game against Barcelona, but up until that point Fulham couldn't really stop him.

Ollie McBurnie (Hull): Grafter, scrappy, endeavour, goals, assists... he had it all in his game in the draw against Ipswich.

He epitomises what Hull are: a player that's always overlooked, a team that's always overlooked, but they've got some spirit and some fight.

Taiwo Awoniyi (Coventry): Unbelievable solo goal. It's really good to see the big fella back playing and being in a situation where he can impose himself. If Coventry are to stay up, he's going to be why.

Frank Lampard (Coventry): He has been really good. Coventry have taken care of business against Sunderland, it was a massive six-pointer and his team came out front-footed, aggressive and also did a job on a very good Sunderland team.

Also a massive nod to Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta for getting the job done at Liverpool.

#855. Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about

The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body

The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times.

That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m.

Which is to say that Fifa, and by extension its all-controlling president Gianni Infantino, was right.

Wrong, mind you, about what it believes anybody with a modicum of taste would think is cool and enjoyable. Like putting Robbie Williams in everything; or cramming Madonna, and BTS, and Shakira, and Justin Bieber, and Ted Lasso, and the Muppets into a World Cup final half-time show that catered to the appetites of the lobotomized; or setting up a pre-final speech on greatness by Tom Cruise.

Wrong, too, about mandatory hydration breaks, and suspending red cards, and stretching the aforementioned, accursed half-time show to 27 minutes in violation of Fifa’s own rules.

But right about all the things Fifa cares about. Which can be neatly reduced to money.

Right that exposing ticket sales – and even parking – to dynamic pricing, driving their prices far out of reach of your average fan, would pay off. Right that it could annex the secondary ticket market and take a hefty cut of resales. Right that the PR hit of cozying up to Donald Trump – who was already deeply unpopular, especially among America’s left-leaning soccer crowd – would not be mortal and, in fact, would not even cost Fifa any money at all. That tolerating the excesses of the Trump government – the disgraceful treatment of the Iranian team, its bluster about potential ICE action around stadiums and its denial of visas to fans and journalists hoping to attend the tournament – would be worth it in order to safeguard the money gusher. (These things may all yet be investigated, among about a million other things, but Fifa’s money is made all the same.)

Right, in the end, that the World Cup is too big to fail. That the decadence and cravenness of the World Cup’s organizers will, in the end, be redeemed by the tournament itself. That the World Cup is unfuckupable.

As things stand, it looks like Infantino may very well survive the fallout of his foolhardy and utterly tone-deaf attempt to quickly and unilaterally sell a chunk of the World Cup’s commercial rights to private equity. That was a bridge too far even in the world’s most cynical sport, but the tournament’s profits appear to have consolidated his power in spite of it all. Infantino has an election to get through in March, but a great many of his ardent supporters are apparently unmoved by the scandal and stand resolutely behind him. While he can’t quite do whatever he wants, it appears he also can’t commit an act grievous enough to be dislodged from power.

As Fifa pointed out to the Athletic, the World Cup’s attendance of 6.8 million was unprecedented – the previous record, from the 1994 World Cup in the United States, was just under 3.6 million. And hat means bigger payouts for Fifa’s 211 member associations, each of which has a presidential-election vote.

This, and only this, is why there is no reforming Fifa until the money stream is somehow slowed. The real power in soccer lies with the money – everything and everyone else is just a figurehead. The sport is organized and optimized to facilitate only the flow of money. We were reminded of this same truth just last week when comments emerged of Kylian Mbappé making light of a meme involving himself and China’s former leader Mao Zedong. The Real Madrid star quickly lost several endorsement deals in China, and scurried to apologize faster than he’s ever loped after a through ball.

Infantino understands this innately and behaves accordingly. And for all his blundering behavior, for all the ugliness and moral insolvency of his grubby masterpiece, the final takeaway from the 2026 World Cup is that, actually, this is all fine. It worked. Pandering to politicians? Proof, meet pudding. The money poured in at an unprecedented flow rate, a rapids of revenue. So, you know, carry on.

And that, to use a term from these lands that have made Fifa even wealthier, sucks.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#854. Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League

Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in England.

"We are absolutely in love with him. He's been an incredible manager. The results are extraordinary and we're flying."

Those words from Ben Parker will be familiar to fans of any club who have been on the kind of winning run Brighton and Hove Albion are currently on.

But all the signs on and off the pitch suggest that the man in question — Brighton's German coach Fabian Hürzeler — is more than just a flash in the Premier League pan.

Hürzeler has never coached in Germany's Bundesliga. After winning promotion to Germany's top flight with St. Pauli in 2024, he left to become the youngest man ever to take charge in England's Premier League at 31. His team currently sit third, having won six games in a row including a 5-0 thrashing of bitter rivals Crystal Palace last weekend.

It was the repeat of a fixture last season that marked Hürzeler's lowest Brighton ebb, with a 1-0 home loss making it one win in 12. "There are only two options," the German coach said at the time. "Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."

Parker, the co-editor of Brighton and Hove Albion fanzine, Dogma, admitted to DW that there were plenty who weren't sure if persisting was the answer. "There was some disquiet at the end of that game, there were people shouting: 'You're getting sacked in the morning.'"

While such sentiment may be difficult to swallow for many coaches, Parker said that Hürzeler told him in an interview soon after joining the club that he welcomed it when needed.

"He talked about wanting a fan relationship that had a two-way aspect. The club and him are really ambitious, so if the performances aren't up to scratch, we should be telling him that. And that's what happened on that day. I see the whole thing as being quite healthy."

Hürzeler never played at the top level. He represented Germany's youth teams and turned out for Bayern Munich's reserves but soon grew frustrated with second-team football. He then accepted a player-coach role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23. From 2018, he was also an assistant coach for Germany's U20s.

He performed this alongside a job at an art dealership in the German state of Bavaria, where he moved with his family at the age of two having been born in the United States. After starting as an assistant coach at St. Pauli in 2020, he took over after head coach Timo Schultz was fired in late 2022. Since then, he hasn't looked back.

That unusual path to top-flight management and some innovative tactics at St. Pauli led to a perception in Germany that Hürzeler was a little aloof and something of a 'laptop manager' in the vein of former Bayern Munich and Germany boss, Julian Nagelsmann who had a similarly nondescript playing career. This, so the charge goes, meant Hürzeler wasn't able to forge the relationships and togetherness needed to make a team more than the sum of its parts.

That was rarely what was reported by his players and staff at St. Pauli, nor is it Hürzeler's belief. "I want to be myself, I don't want to play a role, and my age definitely helps regarding understanding the players," he said.

"I always say I speak their language and I understand their thoughts, because it wasn't that long ago when I played."

His antics on the sideline also earned him a reputation as a bit of a hothead. Hürzeler was booked seven times during St. Pauli's promotion push and since joining Brighton, the German has been booked nine times and been sent off once. When asked about this, he said: "Emotions are part of the game."

Parker said this authenticity has also been reflected in his relationship with Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of England.

"For most Brighton fans he comes across as quite a quirky, interesting, left-field figure. The mantra he set out when he first arrived was quite counter-culturalist, to challenge the establishment, and that fits well here," Parker said.

"You will see him walking along on the seafront, going up for coffees around town, and he travels back and forth on an ebike, not in a chauffer-driven car as a lot of managers might. He's also hosted fan events in pubs, which I believe he paid for. So I'd say he's very approachable."

But Hürzeler isn't the only 30-something German beloved in Brighton.

Pascal Gross, who rejoined the club from Borussia Dortmund in January, is also a firm favorite. The midfielder, who retired from Germany duty after the World Cup earlier this year, has scored three and made four in the club's opening seven league games. The 35-year-old's connection with Hürzeler is also key, with Groß admitting he stayed in touch with Hürzeler even before he resigned. The return is proving to look a great decision for both sides.

"I was here for seven years, got married here and both my kids were born in England. The most important milestones in my life happened here. I missed my friends and the feeling of being deeply connected to the club."

The feeling is mutual, said Parker. "Pascal Gross is everybody's favorite player. He's Brighton's first best signing, from Ingolstadt, and second-best signing, from Dortmund. He's a sensational player, and it's probably true to say there is a lot of warmth towards German football and Germany because of these hugely important characters at the football club."

The Premier League club's success has been built on a smart coach and player recruitment strategy guided by local owner, Tony Bloom. Part of the model is that those who shine brightest will often be snatched by the bigger fish.

"I think he's said he's a supporter of Bayern Munich, and he uses them as an example of the standards he wants," said Parker of Hürzeler. "I can see that he could be a good fit in a couple of years time. He won't go to a Liverpool or a Chelsea, I think there's a strong pull to Bayern in particular."

Bayern's current boss, Vincent Kompany, is in little danger at the moment, though Bayern coaches are only ever a few losses from crisis. For the meantime, Hürzeler is also happy where he is, having extended his contract to 2029. Again, the feeling is mutual.

Next up in the Premier League is a trip to Liverpool, where Jürgen Klopp became the first German coach to make a real mark on the Premier League. But before that, Hürzeler's team have an assignment in the Europa Conference League, a competition Brighton are among the favorites to win. Parker hopes a first major trophy is in sight.

"If he can be the person that wins us that first trophy, then he will go down as the greatest."

Michael J. Fox celebrated his and Tracy Pollan’s daughter Esme on her 25th birthday with sweet photos.

Michael J. Fox still has strong family ties.

The Back to the Future alum recently shared a peek as his and wife Tracy Pollan’s daughter Esme in honor of her 25th birthday.

“Ezzie, you’ve been many people over the last quarter century…all of them fabulous!” Fox wrote in a Nov. 3 Instagram post. “Happy birthday, I love you so much!”

In Fox’s post, he went back and forth from the future, including a photo of his daughter and wife from when she was a little kid, as well as highlights throughout her adulthood including her running the New York City Marathon and graduating from Duke University.

The 65-year-old’s sweet post comes shortly after Esme, as well as his and Pollan’s kids Sam, 37, and twins Aquinnah and Schuyler, both 31, joined him at the Emmys 2026 in September, where he was honored with the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award.

Fox emphasized the support he had received from his family throughout his Parkinson’s diagnosis, thanking them “for their sacrifices, for their patience, and for their love.”

He emphasized of everything his family had gone through since his 1991 diagnosis, “You have no idea.”

Meanwhile, Fox shared that he has been floored by the support he’s received from his audiences as his disease has progressed.

“Support from all of you who are so uplifting and just made me feel like I keep doing this,” he continued. “I hadn't lost what I do and you couldn't take it away from me. And it's because you stood up for me and I appreciate it. Eventually, I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it. “Congratulations to Schuyler, Esme, and all of the Team Fox runners for the love and effort they put into Sunday’s half marathon!” Fox wrote in a March Instagram post. “We’re so proud!”

#851. Lennart Karl steals in behind Atlético Madrid to inspire Bayern Munich win

“This stadium brings back bad memories but I hope to be able to replace them with good ones,” Harry Kane had said on Monday night, and 24 hours later this was a start. A small step, perhaps, towards coming back on 5 June and having a second go at winning the Champions League in the arena where he lost the 2019 final. On his first European outing since winning the Ballon d’Or, the England captain was unable to score but he and his Bayern Munich team defeated Atlético Madrid, fellow semi-finalists from last season. They did so in a way that suggests that their candidacy this season is serious.

It may not have been sparkling but they had been superior almost from the start, dominant in physique and football. This is a team with few weaknesses, intense and impressive throughout. All Atlético could do was resist and it never truly felt like they would be able to do that for ninety minutes; ultimately, they lasted 54. That was when Lennart Karl scored the first. The superb Konrad Laimer then added the second on a night when they racked up nineteen shots. It had been heavy going for a while, and they had been made to wait, but in the end Bayern were just that bit too good.

Although it began with Julián Alvarez bending a shot just wide after 115 seconds, the best picture of the first half was probably the Argentinian’s second shot nineteen minutes later. If that first effort had come from the edge of the area, the chance presenting itself, the second came from the edge of the centre circle, deep inside Atlético’s half and was not so much about opportunity as the lack of them. True, Manuel Neuer was a long way off his line but Alvarez was seventy yards away and his shot never really took flight and was never likely too either, drifting wide.

It was hard to avoid the conclusion that he had gone for it out of a kind of impotence, a desire to do something, anything. Atlético were given so few chances to get near to Neuer’s goal and not very many to get near the ball. There was one moment when a Marc Pubill cross almost reached Alexander Sørloth who couldn’t duck low enough to reach it at the far post, and another when the Norwegian momentarily seemed to have escaped Dayot Upamecano. That, though, was about it. He cut a large and pretty lonely figure.

Paris Saint-Germain set a record as the quickest team to score four goals in the Champions League by powering into a 4-0 lead after 17 minutes against Villarreal on their way to a 6-0 win.

João Neves started the goal-blitz before Desiré Doué, Senny Mayulu and Fabián Ruiz quickly put the tie to bed. Ruiz struck his second to make it 5-0 soon after the interval and substitute David Boly completed the scoring as PSG extended their 100%  Champions League start and moved three points clear at the top of the table.

Since taking just two points from their first three Ligue 1 games this season, which included a 2-1 home defeat to Monaco, PSG have now won 10 successive games in all competitions.

Inter were equally convincing, beating Feyenoord 3-0 at De Kuip. Yann Bisseck curled in the opener from long range, Pio Esposito headed the second before ⁠half-time and Piotr Zielinski completed the scoring from ​distance after ​the restart.

Sporting Lisbon beat Shakhtar Donetsk 1-0, a day after parting ways with their head coach, Rui Borges.  Under the reserve coach, Tiago Fernandes, the Portuguese giants picked up their third win in the Champions League this season, with Issa Doumbia scoring the decisive goal in the game at Stamford Bridge.

Aleksey Batrakov scored two goals in quick succession to seal a 2-0 win for Galatasaray against Stuttgart. Batrakov opened the scoring in the 12th minute at Rams Park and struck again three minutes later. Austria's Lask won 4-0 against Slovan Bratislava and Bodø/Glimt drew 0-0 with Lille

Stadiums across Europe fell silent before kick-off in memory of the Tenerife player Jesús de Miguel, who died earlier on Tuesday after a collision on the pitch in the Spanish second division match against Andorra on Monday. Agencies

Bayern reached the break with almost 70% of the possession, so much of it in a ten or fifteen metre strip along the front of the Atlético area and occasionally inside it. Diego Simeone’s side were gradually pushed further and further back, the frustration of not being allowed into the game growing. And yet that frustration was shared and this had become something of an exercise in patience for both sides: in fact Simeone may have felt some satisfaction at how few spaces his team had allowed Bayern, who prodded and poked and very occasionally got up and running but didn’t find a way through.

Kane was in the middle of many of Bayern’s moves and appeared at the sharp end of them a couple of times. He teed one up for Karl to shoot over, the opportunity opening up for the 18 year old, and had two sights of goal himself. Leaning back, on the turn, Kane volleyed one wide from seven yards. The other came from a similar position when Laimer’s cross had reached Alphonso Davis at the far post. On the turn once again, Kane’s effort was superbly blocked by David Hancko. Josip Stanisic put one wide and Laimer, far more winger than defender, also scuffed a shot when it appeared he was in.

Mostly Bayern were not in, Atlético holding them at the gates. The doubt was always how long that could last, Jan Oblak having to save from Joshua Kimmich just thirty seconds after the restart. Tellingly, that was the keeper’s first stop but Bayern continued. When Tom Bischof stopped a momentary Atlético counter and found Kane soon after, the England captain came in off the left and shot just wide. And then, just nine minutes in, Atlético opened the door they had previously kept locked. Bischof’s deflected shot fell at the feet of Robin Le Normand and Pubill. Neither took responsibility for it; rather they got in each other’s way. Karl took it from them and smuggled it past Oblak.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The game changed there, or appeared to, and Simeone did too: the three substitutions – Lee Kang-in, Koke and Ademola Lookman all came on almost immediately – played their part but perhaps it was more about approach than players. Atlético started to play, get on the ball, and on 65 minutes a smart move and clever ball from Alvarez saw Marcos Llorente turn inside the area and draw a first save from Neuer.

Not that the production was prolific and the risk – the reality too – was that it would also afforded Bayern a little of the space they had been denied before. They seemed to enjoy that, Michael Olise soon sending Laimer up the right wing to fire wide. Atlético meanwhile could not match them. Next Kane shot over. Then Upamecano ran through from deep and struck a deflected shot that hit the bar.

The goal that ended it followed when Davis robbed a tiring Llorente, Kane clipped a neat pass to Laimer on the right and the Austrian had the cool needed to wait for Hancko to slide across to block a feigned shot that didn’t come and then, his dummy bought, smash a shot into the top of the net. There was still time for one more Kane effort, his fifth. That went over but this was done and there will be other days; maybe, he will hope, the biggest day of all, back here again.

#850. Hunger Games’ Mckenna Grace, Joseph Zada React to Fans Shipping Them

Sunrise on the Reaping stars Mckenna Grace and Joseph Zada shared their candid reaction to fans shipping them as a couple in real life: “It’s pretty weird.”

And if fans burn, they want the cast of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to burn with them.

Stars Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace, however, are willing to take it all in stride. And by “it,” we mean fans taking their onscreen bond as Haymitch Abernathy and Maysilee Donner and hoping it becomes romantic IRL.

In reality, the concept made the pair laugh aloud when they were asked about being shipped in an interview.

“Yeah, it’s pretty weird,” Zada said with a smile to Refinery29 Australia, pointing out, “We’ve both got partners.”

He added that Grace feels like his “younger, younger sister,” which made the 20-year-old fire back at her costar, who is only a year older, “Younger? Definitely not.”

But while Zada and Grace may not have volunteered as ship tributes, Grace—who has long had her finger on the pulse of Gen Z internet trends—knows its par for the course in such a big franchise.

“Joe’s like family,” the Gifted star—who is dating her Regretting You costar Mason Thames—said. “I think that’s like the fun of the internet, is that they can ship whatever characters or people or anything that they want as long it’s not intruding on people’s own lives.”

Plus, Zada and Grace were willing to be more than just a piece in fans’ games, offering up alternative ships featuring their costars Ben Wang (who plays District 12 tribute Wyatt Callow), Laura Marcus (District 1 tribute Silka Sharp) and Whitney Peak (Haymitch’s love Lenore Dove).

As Zada noted, “I’ve been shipped with Ben, and like I can see that,” to which Grace added, “Honestly, my favorite ship is Ben and Joe.”

And when Zada suggested Marcus and Grace could also be a good ship, she offered up a challenge to her costar.

“I like Maydove,” she said, referring to her and Peak’s characters Maysilee and Lenore. “I’m coming for your girl.”

But not only does Grace have decades in the spotlight preparing her for this moment, but she also received advice from the boy with the bread, Josh Hutcherson, who played Peeta Mellark in the original movies and whom Grace starred alongside in Five Nights at Freddy’s 2.

As she revealed, Hutcherson was a wonderful sounding board as she prepared herself to step into the Hunger Games fandom.

“I just talk to Josh a lot because we were on that press tour together and spent a lot of time together,” she told E! News at the Coach Fall 2026 show on Feb. 11. “I spent a lot of time asking him, ‘Was your arena experience as intense as ours was?’ And he was like, ‘Oh yeah, yeah it was.’”

But while Zada and Grace have not dated, nor are they ever likely to, they’re not the only costars who have found themselves the subject of dating speculation. Read on for more costars whose relationships were strictly platonic—despite fans’ hopes to the contrary.

The Anyone But You costars may have found love onscreen, but that's where it stayed. Despite the onslaught of dating rumors amid their 2023 press tour, the pair emphasized that their relationship was strictly platonic.

"The two things that you have to sell a rom-com are fun and chemistry," Glen told the New York Times in April 2024. "Sydney and I have a ton of fun together, and we have a ton of effortless chemistry. That's people wanting what's on the screen off the screen, and sometimes you just have to lean into it a bit—and it worked wonderfully. Sydney is very smart."

Meanwhile, Sydney—who was engaged to businessman Jonathan Davino at the time, though they split in March 2025 after seven years together—asserted that she and Glen didn't play up their chemistry ahead of the rom-com's release.

"Honestly, the press did it themselves. There was no leaning in, per se," she told Variety in October 2025. "Truly, the tabloids and journalists just created it and kept going."

"Glen and I genuinely care for each other and have a love and respect for one another," she emphasized. "I love being with him. And I think people just truly saw a really beautiful pairing."

Hermione Granger and Draco Malfoy?! If Emma had it her way, the Harry Potter franchise would have had a Hogwarts House-crossed romance going down off-screen. The actress has admitted to nursing a serious crush on her bleached blonde co-star.During the Harry Potter 20th anniversary special, Emma shared that as a child she "fell in love" with Tom while on the set of their first film together, Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone. "I used to come in every day and look for his number on the call sheet, it was No. 7, and if his name was on the call sheet, it was an extra exciting day," she said during the reunion. "He was three years above me and so for him he was like, 'You're like my little sister.'"Shortly after the special premiered, fans of the series quickly took to the Internet to share their wish for the longtime friends to become something more.However, in an interview with British Vogue, Emma addressed the online reaction and put any potential dating rumors to rest. "We speak most weeks," she said, "and we just think it's sweet."

"We respected that."Jennifer added, "Honestly, I remember saying one time to David, 'It's going to be such a bummer if the first time you and I actually kiss is going to be on national television.' And sure enough, the first time we kissed was in that coffee shop."So, instead of having a romance IRL, she explained that they "just channeled all of our adoration and love for each other into Ross and Rachel."

Arguably one of the most iconic pairings in movie history, fans have shipped Leo and Kate together since 1996's Titanic (even though she didn't make room for him on that door). Still, they never let go of their friendship, with Kate telling The Guardian last year that they are "bonded for life." From walking the red carpet together at the 1998 Golden Globes to watching DiCaprio blow kisses to Winslet during her emotional 2009 Golden Globes speech, it's so evident that the feelings between the besties have only continued to grow over the past two decades, iceberg be damned.

The unexpected pairing's chemistry in 2019's A Star Is Born and its ensuing press tour made fans blind to the fact that the actor and director was dating Irina Shayk and the pop star was engaged to Christian Carano at the time.Still, it was clear that the costars had a close bond, with Gaga revealing that she had an "instant connection" with Bradley that came "the second that I saw him."Of course, that closeness was on full display when the pair took to the Oscars stage in 2019, hand-in-hand, to perform their Best Song-winning number, "Shallow," just days after Gaga ended her engagement.

During a Q&A session at the 2018 Telluride Film Festival, the Cruella star revealed how much Ryan meant to her and his impact on her life and career. Calling him a "dear, wonderful friend," Emma said, "I can't even imagine what my life would be without Ryan.
