#795. NFL's Jack Campbell Breaks Silence After Suffering Serious Neck Injury

Following Detroit Lions star Jack Campbell’s serious neck injury during the team’s Nov. 1 game, which appeared to leave him unable to move, the linebacker shared a positive update on his mobility.

Jack Campbell is calling a huddle of his own.

Three days after the Detroit Lions linebacker suffered an immobilizing neck injury and was carried off the field on a stretcher, he broke his silence to deliver a positive update.

“I’m incredibly encouraged by the progress I’ve made in such a short period of time,” Campbell shared in a statement to the Lions’ Instagram Nov. 4. “I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body.”

Still, the 26-year-old added, “I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”

Since sustaining the injury during the fourth quarter of the team’s 19-15 triumph over the Minnesota Vikings—which left him lying face down on the field, seemingly unable to move at the time—Campbell noted he’s been leaning on his faith in God.

“I know He has a plan for me, and I trust in that plan,” the athlete continued. “I know there may be challenges ahead, but with my faith, my family, and so many people in my corner, I know we’ll get through this.”

Amid his recovery, the University of Iowa alum also emphasized how grateful he and his family—including his wife Megan and their 4-month-old son Cooper—are for the “overwhelming” support they’ve received from fans.

Plus, Campbell gave a special shoutout to the medical staff who have treated him.

“I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field,” he wrote. “I know those were difficult moments, and I'm incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I'll never forget.”

As the NFL star put it, “From the bottom of my heart, thank you.”

While sharing that he plans to “approach this challenge” with the “toughness, resilience and grit” that Detroit is built upon, Campbell turned his focus to his team.

“To my teammates, coaches, and everyone in the Lions organization, I want you to know how much I love and appreciate you,” he shared. “This team is a family to me, and the way everyone has been there for me means everything. I'm proud to be a Detroit Lion and couldn't ask to be surrounded by a better group of people.”

For all the details to know about Campbell’s neck injury, keep reading…

Jack Campbell was injured during the Detroit Lions’ Nov. 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings

In the fourth quarter of the teams' match-up, Campbell tackled opponent T.J. Hockenson—his third tackle of the game—and was hit on the way down.

He lay face-down on the field, unable to move after the play, and had to be carried off on a backboard by medical personnel.

Campbell was rushed to a nearby hospital to have his neck evaluated

A reporter present at the game called Campbell’s hit the “scariest moment” he’d ever witnessed at Ford Field in a Nov. 1 post on X. He also confirmed that Campbell’s wife Megan Campbell and their baby boy Cooper, who was born in July 2026, were brought down to the field to accompany the player in an ambulance.

Lions coach Dan Campbell—who has no relation to the linebacker—said the team was “thinking about him” in a post-game interview, but had no information to share.

In a post on X following the game, the Detroit Lions confirmed that Campbell was brought “to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury.”

Campbell has remained hospitalized following his injury

On Nov. 2, the Detroit Lions confirmed that Campbell was being closely monitored at the hospital.

“Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital,” the team wrote in a post on X. “Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.”

Lions coach says Campbell’s recovery update is “positive”

In a press conference one day after Campbell’s injury, Coach Campbell confirmed a heartening update on his player’s recovery.

“It’s positive,” he said. “Your prayers are working. Please continue to do that. We’ll leave it at that. Just continue to pray for him but it is positive news on Jack.”

Coach Campbell calls player an “unbelievable person”

While addressing his player’s injury, the Detroit Lions coach emphasized Campbell’s impact on the team, especially after he was tapped as team captain for this season.

“I don’t even know if I can put it into words,” Dan said during a press conference Nov. 2. “You get voted captain, that says a ton, especially with this group of guys that has been assembled. He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy, he’s dependable. He’d give you the shirt off his back. He’s just all heart, man. All effort."

As he put it, “There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him,”

In an appearance on 97.1 The Ticket Radio Show Nov. 3, Coach Campbell shared an update on his player’s recovery.

“It’s not easy because he’s going to always be on our minds over here,” he said. “The good news is he is improving.”

Campbell breaks silence, says he is "very optimistic" about progress

The linebacker shared a positive update Nov. 4, noting he is "encouraged by the progress" he has made in the three days since his injury.

“I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body,” he wrote in a statement shared to the Detroit Lions' Instagram. "I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”

#793. The oracle of the second quadrant

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chao Liu has driven up and down the US East Coast — from Florida to Massachusetts — before detouring to France. His latest stop is at IFREMER, where he will continue to pretend to be a real scientist until someone finally catches on.

The machine sat between the deep-fryer truck and a three-legged goat, housed inside a canvas tent that smelled heavily of kerosene and stale popcorn. It was a massive, rivet-popped iron boiler known officially as the Differential Analytical Oscillator, although the hand-painted sign out front simply read: THE DAO BOILER — KNOWS ALL, TELLS ALL. FIVE CENTS.

By late afternoon, the fairground was a soup of churned mud and diesel exhaust.

“It don’t do lottery numbers,” the operator said, not looking up from the greasy carburettor he was scraping with a butter knife. He was a small, sour man named Silas, wearing a leather apron stiff with soot. “And if you’re gonna ask if your brother’s a bastard, save your nickel. The answer is always yes.”

Jerry shifted his boots in the sawdust. He was 19, wore a stained canvas jacket, and had spent the past three days trying to look tragically heartbroken on his front porch. “I don’t care about the lottery. I want to know about Clara.”

Silas sighed, spitting a dark stream of tobacco juice into a bucket of scrap iron. “The butcher’s girl? She left on the 4.10 rail to Lowmarsh. What’s to know? She wanted indoor plumbing and a man who didn’t smell like fertilizer.”

“No,” Jerry said, his jaw tightening as he dropped a heavy brass nickel onto the tool chest. “She said it wasn’t that. She said there was a … a fundamental misalignment in our vectors. I want to know what that means. I want the real, exact reason.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Silas looked at the coin, then at Jerry’s face. He let out a dry, rattling chuckle. “The exact reason? All right, kid. But the tub don’t do poetry. You want the low-voltage ribbon or the full squeeze?”

“Give me the whole thing,” Jerry said, crossing his arms. “Don’t spare the details.”

Silas shrugged, picking up a heavy, lead-lined copper helmet attached to the boiler by a thick bundle of rubber-coated cables. It looked like an old diving apparatus, dripping with mineral oil. “Put it on. Full throttle means you get the absolute breakdown. Don’t say I didn’t warn you.”

Jerry lifted the helmet. It was incredibly heavy, cold against his ears. He lowered it over his head, plunging himself into absolute darkness.

For three seconds, there was only the smell of hot grease and the rhythmic thump-thump-thump of the internal pistons. Then, the engine engaged the clutch.

The Universe didn’t open up with grand spiritual enlightenment. It opened with a relentless, deafening avalanche of raw data.

Jerry didn’t see Clara’s face, or a vision of her on the train. Instead, a cold, mechanical voice began reading a molecular ledger directly into his auditory cortex. It informed him that on Tuesday at 3.14 p.m., the atmospheric humidity had caused a 0.04% swelling in the leather of Clara’s left boot, which altered her gait by three millimetres. This structural variance, combined with the gravitational pull of a passing manure spreader, had shifted her centre of gravity exactly enough to cause a microscopic tear in the cotton fibre of her socks.

The machine kept going. It explained that the chemical composition of Jerry’s afternoon sweat contained an excess of sulfur molecules that reacted poorly with the zinc coating on his porch railing, creating a localized scent profile that her olfactory nerves categorized under Sub-Class 4: Decaying Organic Matter. It gave him the exact thermodynamic equation of the breeze that had carried the smell to her nose. It gave him the precise atomic mass of the dust particle she choked on when she tried to say goodbye.

It went on for what felt like an eternity, resolving her ‘broken heart’ into a massive, agonizingly boring list of friction coefficients, cellular degeneration rates and barometric pressure shifts. There was no love. There was no betrayal. There was only a three-hour maths problem about why a girl walked towards a train station.

The helmet was violently yanked off his head.

Jerry stumbled backwards, blinking against the harsh light of the tent. The machine was smoking, its violet glow dying back into a dull, rusted grey. Silas was standing over him, holding the helmet, looking thoroughly bored.

#792. Championship roundup: West Ham stage dramatic comeback on Scott Parker’s opening night

West Ham recover from 3-0 down to draw 3-3 at Cardiff

Leaders Middlesbrough beaten 2-0 at Wrexham

Scott Parker’s return to West Ham had had looked like beginning in painful fashion but instead featured a stunning comeback from 3-0 down. The east London club’s new head coach had watched Cardiff’s Jack Moylan score a first-half hat-trick, before a rousing response after the break ended with Max Kilman levelling the scores at 3-3 eight minutes from time. Elsewhere in the Championship, the leaders Middlesbrough went down 2-0 at Wrexham.

Parker had been confirmed as West Ham’s head coach earlier on Wednesday, taking over from Nuno Espírito Santo, who was sacked on Tuesday. The club’s former midfielder was appointed on a two-and-a-half-year contract.

Moylan halted the initial feelgood factor among the visiting support in the 11th minute at Cardiff City Stadium. His right-foot drive from the tip of the D left the visiting goalkeeper Mads Hermansen helpless as it sped into the top left corner. Moylan was then brought down for a penalty – the Ireland midfielder got up to spank it home to the left as Hermansen dived right in the 37th minute.

Within two minutes, Will Fish thought he had turned in a corner for Cardiff’s third – the centre-back deftly headed towards goal, but Moylan was directly behind him and claimed his hat-trick after making the final touch.

After the break, it was a completely different story. Divine Mukasa reduced the deficit in the 58th minute, finishing calmly over the stranded Nathan Trott after a fine ball over the top from Jarrod Bowen, before Arne Engels capitalised on a mix-up in the home defence to make it 3-2.

In the 82nd minute, Bowen was again the supplier, curling in an inviting cross from the right that was turned in by the centre-back Kilman to make it 3-3 from close range.

At the Racecourse, Wrexham waited until the 70th minute to break the deadlock against Middlesbrough, before George Thomason smashed a shot into the ground from just outside the area, which rocketed past a crowd of defenders and through the unsighted visiting goalkeeper Radek Vítek. Oli Rathbone then made it 2-0 in the 84th minute.

#791. Russia's attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, are intensifying. DW asked people on the ground what life is like

Russia's attacks on the Ukrainian capital are hitting harder and more frequently, making 2026 one of the long war's bloodiest years for Kyiv. DW asked people on the ground what life is like.

Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine. Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city.

With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv, subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls.

"We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months.

In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel.

Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building  in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time.

"We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said.

Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day.

"This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone."

"Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks.

In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said.

Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.

Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter.

Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.

Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This  could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.

“I was growing you inside of me and at the same time you were giving me life!” she added. “You gave a new meaning to what a Grey day feels like. You light up my life and every room with your smile your laugh and your precious spirit.”

"My boyfriend at the time—he dumped me two weeks before my prom, but I honestly think it was because he didn't want to pay for the limo, but then that night…forget it," she told Jimmy Fallon and John Mulaney on The Tonight Show. "The limo that I ended up with—I didn't rented it…I just got in a limo and just…forget it. I can't get into it. Kids watch me now."

"Once you start making money, everybody wants you to be their kid's godmother," she quipped on The Tonight Show.

"I want to thank my fans—Bardi Gang—because even when I'm wrong they be like, 'She still right' and I want to thank my haters, too, because they be downloading my stuff so they can hear it and talk crap about it, but it benefits me!" she said while accepting the Best New Artist Award at the 2018 iHeartRadio Music Awards.

"I'm just a regular, degular, shmegular girl from the Bronx," the former reality star has said often on Love & Hip Hop.

"If he has sex with you more than five times, he loves you," she told BET in 2017.

"I'm feeling good, I'm feeling nervous, overwhelmed—everything!" she told E!'s Giuliana Rancic at the 2018 Grammys. "Butterflies in my stomach and vagina!"

"I get really happy when people see me perform and they're rapping my music, but it's a different feeling when you're dancing and the men throwing you money because you look good," she told New York in 2017. "It's just like when the rice is getting thrown at the bride."

"Sometimes I get a little discouraged, and I wonder how it is going to be next year, but it seems like everybody already predicting where I'm gonna be next year, and it's just like f--king farther than my a--hole," she told New York in 2017.

In a candid Instagram video, Cardi said, "You know, as I get older and I wax more I notice that my mustache is getting thicker. But it's cool though, cause b--ches with good mustaches got good p---y."

#787. Champions League: Como clobber Lens 9-1 after Real Madrid roar back to deny AEK Athens

Valverde hits late winner as Madrid win 3-2 in Athens

Napoli thrashed by Porto, Club Brugge win at PSV

Anastasios Douvikas led the rout with a hat-trick as Como cruised to a 9-1 victory away at Lens, equalling the record for the most goals scored in a single Champions League game.

Only two teams had previously won a game by a margin of eight goals since the launch of the modern Champions League in 1992.

Liverpool thumped Besiktas 8-0 in the group stage in 2007 and Real Madrid won by the same scoreline against Malmo in 2015.

Como are just the second team to score nine times in a game in the competition, after Bayern Munich beat Dinamo Zagreb 9-2 in the league phase in 2024.

Cesc Fabregas’s side made it three wins from four in their maiden campaign in the competition with a spellbinding display.

Nico Paz continued his fine form with a goal and two assists, while Lucas Da Cunha, Marc-Oliver Kempf, Mattia Liberali, Martin Baturina and Matteo Papaccioli also scored for the Serie A side, who had already beaten both RB Leipzig and Manchester United 4-1 at home in this campaign.

The last club to score nine away from home in the European Cup was Feyenoord against Olympiakos in 1971.

Federico Valverde lashed home a stunning effort from distance to snatch Real Madrid a late 3-2 victory at AEK Athens on Wednesday and preserve their 100% start in the group phase.

José Mourinho’s side, who started with Vinícius Júnior on the left flank after he missed the team’s previous two La Liga matches through suspension, twice came from behind against the Greek champions before Valverde claimed all three points for his side.

Aboubakary Koïta sent AEK ahead after 12 minutes before Jude Bellingham equalised with a sublime flick for the record 15-time winners.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Stavros Pilios sent the Greek champions ahead with 15 minutes to go but Kylian Mbappé swiftly pulled Madrid level once again, setting the stage for Valverde’s late winner.

Madrid have now won seven straight games across all competitions.

Scott McTominay found the net but Napoli suffered a 4-1 defeat by Porto, who had lost their first three games in the competition, while Club Brugge are up to ninth after a 2-1 win at PSV.

Konstantinos Karetsas struck a 72nd-minute winner as Borussia Dortmund beat Real Betis 2-1 while Erik Botheim helped himself to two goals as Viking secured their first triumph with a 4-1 win over 10-man Sabah.

#785. Andrew Garfield Addresses Family Plans Amid Monica Barbaro Romance

Andrew Garfield, who has been dating Monica Barbaro since 2024, addressed whether he still has plans to start a family and have any kids of his own, saying, “It’s mysterious to me.”

Andrew Garfield isn’t sure if he wants to keep spinning his family’s web.

The Amazing Spider-Man alum recently detailed whether he still has plans to start a family or have kids in the near future, admitting he still isn’t feeling definitive either way.

“I’m the same as everyone else who’s even remotely cognizant of where we are and where we’re heading,” Garfield explained in an interview with GQ published Nov. 4. “I look at my friends who do have kids and the beauty of it obviously, but also the struggle of it and the inescapable agony of young people’s longing to belong to the screen rather than belong to the real world.”

Garfield—who has been in a relationship with Monica Barbaro since 2024—admitted that he has no Spidey sense when it comes to whether having kids is a good idea.

“It gives me pause for sure, like any person, I suppose,” he continued. “That being said, there is that kind of biological imperative, and there is that just kind of instinct, and there’s an image that your life with for so long—I have, anyway—of the concept of being a dad and going on an adventure.”

At 43, Garfield has been more vocal with the concept of having kids at some point.

“I’m childless,” he said during a September appearance on the Smartless podcast. “I’m not entirely proud of that. I would love to have kids. I would love to start a family.”

But while the We Live in Time actor—who previously dated Emma Stone and Dr. Kate Tomas—has taken off his mask when it comes to discussing the potential of having future children, he recently drew the line when it came to discussing his romantic life.

“It feels like a violation of my inner world, my private world,” Garfield explained in an interview with Vanity Fair last year. “I thought maybe that would soften at some point, but I’m very surprised to say that it hasn’t.”

He firmly acknowledged, “I have never, and I won’t ever, speak about or confirm or deny anything about my personal life with anyone.”

If you're Spidey senses are tingling for more details, keep reading for a look back at Garfield's love life.

If you've been on the internet, then you're aware those romance rumors about Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro aren't a complete unknown.The We Live in Time actor and the A Complete Unknown actress sparked dating speculation after a social media user shared a video of the pair attending Jonathan Bailey's performance of Richard II at London's Bridge Theatre Feb. 19.However, this wouldn't be the first time Monica and Andrew had crossed paths. They were also photographed alongside Eddie Redmayne and W Magazine's Editor-at-Large Lynn Hirschberg at the outlet's Annual Best Performances Party in Los Angeles January 4.E! News reached out to Monica and Andrew's reps for comment but didn't hear back.

Fans' social networks alerted them to Andrew's romance with Dr. Kate Tomas after the two were seen on an apparent double date with Phoebe Bridgers and Bo Burnham in March 2024.“I am in a new relationship," the spiritual mentor said on a June 2024 episode of her podcast The Friday Emails without naming names, per The Sunday Times, "and I’m in love and I’m really happy."However, she didn't love that the media mostly focused on her relationship with the Oscar nominee."It’s frustrating that no matter how accomplished or impactful a woman is, it’s always going to be more interesting if they are in a relationship with a man," Kate told The Sunday Times in a July 2024 interview. Emma Stone and Andrew's bond went from friendly, neighborhood costars to a loving couple after they worked together on The Amazing Spider-Man in 2011."It's a dream to work with him," the Oscar winner said in a 2014 interview with ABC News. Still, the La La Land star—who is now married to Dave McCary— and the Mainstream actor continue to be on good terms.

"We care about each other so much, and that’s a given, that’s kind of this unconditional thing,” he said on a 2017 episode of Vanity Fair's Little Gold Men podcast. “There’s so much love between us and so much respect...I’m her biggest fan as an artist. So for me, it’s been bliss to be able to watch her success and watch her bloom into the actress that she is. And it’s also been wonderful to have that kind of support for each other. It’s nothing but a beautiful thing.”

"I think my girlfriend is proud of me and the fact that I've remained grounded," he told Parade in 2010, the year of the film's debut. "I think I'm just busier. That's the main thing. I haven't got as much time to mope about and complain that I'm bored. She travels with me when she's not working. Whenever we have time, we're together. When I'm on my own, you'd find me in the ocean surfing."

But after three years together, the Under the Banner of Heaven alum and the Raising Hope actress parted ways.

#783. Erling Haaland settles thriller for Manchester City to end RB Leipzig resistance

Feed Erling Haaland and Manchester City’s totemic No 9 will score. The problem, recently, has been a paucity of openings for him.

This was true again before Elliot Anderson crossed and Haaland slid home a priceless winner for Enzo Maresca’s disjointed unit, Rayan Cherki hitting a post late on.

The win ends City’s sequence of two losses in three games yet the manager has major issues. He has to plug a leaky defence and drill his midfield to exert control.

And there is a shaky Gianluigi Donnarumma: City’s goalkeeper was culpable for Ridle Baku’s first equaliser for Leipzig, as he was for Nicolas Jackson’s winner in the recent defeat at Aston Villa, plus two more in last month’s Paris Saint-Germain loss.

The manager said: “It’s not a concern but it’s a mistake. But in 48 hours [Saturday] we have Nottingham Forest away, we need to be focused on that and then in the international break I will look. At the moment I’m not thinking about the goalkeeping situation. Gigio knows he was not good with the first goal.”

He was honest, too, about Antonio Nusa’s second for Leipzig, the forward taking advantage of a lax rearguard. “Both goals are quite silly goals we can avoid,” said Maresca.

Still, after going down to Villa and Brighton in the Premier League, the win is a certifiable tonic ahead of the Forest trip.

City’s quest to return to victorious ways featured an XI of four changes from Saturday’s Brighton reverse. Noteworthy was Maresca’s dropping of Rúben Dias as Abdukodir Khusanov’s pace was preferred at centre-back to the captain, Haaland taking the armband.

While the 2,000-plus travelling support were stationed in a quadrant to the right of Donnarumma’s goal, the noise came from the congregation behind Maarten Vandevoordt’s where a sea of red and white bounced to the tempo of a booming drum. They could roar particularly loud when Nusa flitted across City’s D and unloaded and what should have been a regulation save for Donnarumma became a fumble – and corner for Leipzig.

As can be with this Maresca unit, control was difficult to find and administer for any prolonged passage: Phil Foden twice lost the ball when turning into traffic was no aid, the second time meaning Nusa could zigzag towards goal.

The Brighton defeat featured close to zero service for Haaland and City’s 13-goal man was again hard to find, Matheus Nunes’ loose cross, when the captain lurked, emblematic. So, too, as a sign of Leipzig’s ascendancy, was Marc Guéhi scrambling to clear danger, Nusa firing in the ball from the left, and Christoph Baumgartner having space to shoot marginally wide of Donnarumma’s left post.

“Keep the ball and shift it faster” might have been Maresca’s instruction and when this happened City fashioned the breakthrough.

Cherki speared a diagonal right-left into a galloping Nico O’Reilly, whose instant cross caused Castello Lukeba to panic and turn home, via a trailing left knee. City had forced the issue and twice went close to a second moments later.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

First, O’Reilly floated the ball into Leipzig’s area but Haaland’s header faltered. Then the left-back was set up by Iliman Ndiaye’s cross only for O’Reilly to miss with the same part of his anatomy.

Yet as the second half began Leipzig were staring at a fifth defeat in the fixture, having won only once in six previous meetings, all in this competition.

Intent was signalled by Nusa’s mazy run along the left, his chip causing Donnarumma to push away when he might have caught. This roused the home fans and better followed for their team – but not Donnarumma.

Anderson’s loose ball for O’Reilly near halfway was snaffled by Leipzig, who marauded down the right before Brajan Gruda fed an overlapping Baku. Now, came Donnarumma’s folly because, while the right-back’s shot was true, it was steered along a very tight angle, yet City’s No 1 allowed it to go in between him and his left post.

Here was the latest goal-costing error from the Italian – one for Maresca to ponder. Yet 1-1 was still a fair result away from the Etihad Stadium so relief emanated from those in black when Ezechiel Banzuzi’s shot hit side-netting only. Donnarumma’s wobble continued, though, as he fumbled another Baku attempt, narrowly recovering.

City were about to show character and quality: Ndiaye’s pinpoint cross from the left had Enzo Fernández arriving to head in supremely and Maresca’s team led again. Not for long. Leipzig waltzed through with ease and with Nunes out of position, Nusa finished expertly from the left.

After Anderson skied over from close-range, Haaland did what makes him so lethal: net his sole chance. “Not sure how many touches I had, but most important is that I managed to help the team to win,” said the Norwegian.

#782. Dakota Johnson, Machine Gun Kelly Hit a High Note With Dinner Date

Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly stepped out for a dinner date in Calabasas, Calif., on Nov. 3, continuing to fuel romance rumors with another public outing.

There’s nothing grey about Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly’s chemistry

That’s because the Madame Web actress and “blood valentine” artist added more fuel to relationship speculation when they enjoyed another joint outing together at a restaurant in Calabasas, Calif., on Nov. 3.

The pair—who first sparked romance rumors in September—were all smiles, grinning at one another as they waited for their car at valet outside the establishment.

For their dinner date, Johnson kept her look effortlessly chic, wearing a black leather jacket with a fur collar with a pair of light washed jeans. She styled her dark locks in a loose updo with a claw clip. To accessorize, the Fifty Shades of Grey star made a statement with an animal-print handbag.

As for MGK (real name Colson Baker), he rocked a casual ensemble, sporting salmon pink sweatpants and a dark gray shirt, with a hoodie and black bomber jacket on top.

Although neither the “Bad Things” singer nor Verity star have yet to comment on dating rumors, this marks the latest of several outings for the pair in recent weeks.

After all, Johnson, 37, and MGK, 36, first made waves when they stepped out together on Sept. 12 in New York City nearly a month after the Social Network actress’ split from Role Model was confirmed.

The duo further fueled speculation when Johnson supported MGK as he walked the runway at Milan Fashion Week’s Vogue World 2026 show on Sept. 22.

And it was just a few weeks later that the Materialists star and “Lonely Road” artist said yes to another romantic outing, with the pair seen arriving to Hollywood speakeasy Say Yes on Oct. 14.

Although she’s created a web of conversation with her love life, Johnson—who previously dated Coldplay’s Chris Martin from 2017 until 2025—jokingly alluded that she may have a type when it comes to musicians.

While Vogue pointed out in a Sept. 18 interview that the Suspiria star does “know a lot of musicians,” she quipped, “They like me. I don’t know what to say.”

After Johnson noted that she “like[s] them” too, the interviewer asked, “What’s not to like?” to which the Bigger Splash actress had a cheeky remark ready to go.

“A lot! A lot,” she joked. “Tricky motherf--kers.”

#780. Viktor Gyökeres the difference as Arsenal claim nervy win against Slavia Prague

Another European away day, another victory for Arsenal: albeit only just. This time, Viktor Gyökeres stole the show as poor Slavia Prague matched the longest winless streak in European Cup and Champions League history despite a spirited late comeback. That unwanted record stands at 23, equalling the mark set by AEK Athens and FCSB – formerly known as Steaua Bucharest – while Arsenal are unbeaten in their 10 last away trips. But had it not been for a wonder save from David Raya, the Czech champions would have snatched a point after Wiktor Nowak pulled one back late on as Mikel Arteta’s usually watertight defence showed signs of fallibility under pressure.

In contrast to last week’s defeat against Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup, Arsenal had been cruising until the last 15 minutes after Noni Madueke fired them ahead early on, set up superbly by Gyökeres.

That was the Sweden striker’s third assist in his past five appearances, although Arteta will have been even more encouraged by the emphatic finish that appeared to put the game beyond Slavia’s reach just before the break.

But the Arsenal manager admitted his side had taken their eye off the ball by allowing their hosts back into the game with some uncharacteristic defensive lapses as Slavia racked up 18 shots to his side’s 12.

“At half-time, the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game,” said Arteta. “We were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept and in everything that we discussed to avoid the game that we played in the second half. That is a huge learning.”

Slavia’s solitary victory in this competition came in their first-ever match in 2007 and after losing 3-0 to Arsenal here exactly a year ago, they knew their chances of avoiding the unwanted milestone were extremely slim. Arteta’s side have developed a killer instinct on their travels in Europe – not since May 2025 in the second leg of their semi-final against Paris Saint-Germain have Arsenal lost an away game in 90 minutes.

After their exploits at Anfield on Sunday that took them three points clear at the top of the Premier League, Arteta heavily rotated his side again with six changes. It’s perhaps not surprising that Martín Zubimendi ran out of steam given the Spain World Cup winner made only his third start of a frustrating campaign.

For the third time in Arsenal’s past four matches, Gyökeres was entrusted with leading the line after finally getting off the mark with a scrappy strike against Fleetwood. He finished as top scorer last season with 21 goals but has clearly been struggling for form and confidence. Yet there was no doubting the quality of his assist for Madueke’s opening goal after just eight minutes.

Raya’s long ball should have been dealt with by the Slavia defence but they made the criminal error of ­allowing it to bounce. That was the cue for Gyökeres to come alive as he beat his marker to the ball, chested it down and played the perfect pass for the England forward to run on to and score. Arteta’s reaction on the touchline suggested he enjoyed it too.

Mikel Merino was Arsenal’s hero here last year with two goals and he could have extended their lead on three occasions before the half-hour mark. The lively Madueke created his best opportunity after cutting the ball back to Merino but he could not beat Nazar Domchak in Slavia’s goal.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

With Martin Ødegaard watching from the bench next to William Saliba on his return from a long-term back injury, Arsenal lacked some of their usual fluency in attack. But ­Slavia were still no match for them and their task became almost ­impossible seven minutes before the break. Gyökeres exchanged a smart one-two with Merino inside the area before curling a brilliant shot into the far corner.

To their credit, the hosts began the second half with much more aggression after introducing their record signing, Ange N’Guessan, from the bench. Ezri Konsa and Declan Rice both found themselves in the book as Arsenal were pinned back. David Jurasek let fly from long range and his effort was deflected just wide of Raya’s goal. From the resulting corner, Gabriel Magalhães somehow managed to clear two goalbound headers off the line in a matter of seconds. The Brazilian celebrated with a massive fist pump but his evening wasn’t over.

Mikulas Konecny should have done much better with another header before Raya managed to push Oskar Kubiak’s header on to the post despite being at full stretch in mid-air. Slavia eventually scored the goal all their endeavour deserved in the final minute of normal time when Nowak fired in at the far post. There were a few nervous moments in stoppage time as Konecny forced Raya into another save. Arteta breathed a sigh of relief at the full-time whistle as Slavia were condemned to their fate.

#779. Tara Lipinski Admits She's Unsure About Daughter's Skating Future

Big Bargain Holiday Showdown host Tara Lipinski shared insight into her 3-year-old daughter Georgie’s passion for skating in an exclusive E! News interview: "I just want it to be all fun."

Tara Lipinski is surprised how her daughter is skating to her own tune.

The Olympic figure skater shared that while it's been incredibly heartwarming to watch her and husband Todd Kapostasy’s 3-year-old Georgie take to the ice, she’s not sure if she wants her daughter joining the world of competitive figure skating.

“I never really want her to ever feel pressure to ever follow in my footsteps,” Lipinski exclusively told E! News. “So part of me really never thought she would skate. And I don't know if I actually want her to skate.”

However, Georgie has really found her footing on the ice, with Lipinski joking, “The problem is she likes it.”

For now, the 44-year-old is going to encourage the fun part of skating, adding that getting involved in sports is also “a great confidence builder” that can “give you so many tools that you use later in life.”

“If she loves it as much as she does, we'll do it for as long as she wants,” Lipinski said, sharing that Georgie “loves the sparkly outfits, and she loves the sequins, and skating to 'Pink Pony Club.’”

“I just want it to be all fun,” she emphasized. “I obviously saw how serious a sport can get, and for Georgie I just want her to see all the positive aspects of being on the ice and having fun.”

Of course, the Olympic gold medalist is doing her best to keep the fun skating along for Georgie, especially with the holidays coming up.

“We are in prime magical Christmas memories and moments and she is so into it,” Lipinski raved. “I even told her this morning, I was like, ‘It's time to decorate for Christmas,’ and you can see the little smile pop up.”

Luckily, she’s got plenty of inspiration for her holiday decor as the host of HGTV’s Big Bargain Holiday Showdown, in which contestants are challenged to create Christmastime magic on a dime.

“I had a little notepad that I, eventually, after the second episode, was like, ‘Oh, I'm going to take notes on this. I don't need to spend money to do that. Now I can do it like this,’” she shared. “The added benefit of the show is that we get to see how it's done on a budget and that it's relatable, so that everyone at home can try fun projects when it comes to their decorating this year.”

And the sports commentator was truly dazzled by how the competitors stuck the landing on the series, raving, “It was incredible to see how the teams were able to come up with these creative and unique ideas.”

Big Bargain Holiday Showdown airs on HGTV Tuesday nights starting Nov. 3 at 9 p.m. ET.

For a look at more shows headed to the small screen this year, keep reading.

Nocturne tells the story of Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber), an ex-soldier turned homicide detective who, tired of working the tough streets of Philadelphia, moves to a small town in Western Pennsylvania for a quiet life. The Remarried Princess (Hulu & Disney+) - Nov. 4

Based on the hit Naver Webtoon of the same name, The Remarried Empress follows the strained relationship of beloved Empress Navier and her husband Emperor Sovieshu of the Eastern Kingdom. With anxieties rising across the kingdom, the couple’s relationship begins to fracture when Sovieshu falls in love with a runaway slave and attempts to move heaven and earth to win her heart. Unwilling to compromise her dignity, Navier acquiesces to the emperor’s requests on one condition – that she be allowed to remarry rival Crown Prince Heinrey of the Western Kingdom. What follows is a tale of love, lust and regret that threatens the fate of an entire kingdom as Navier strives to reclaim her power.

Taken: Natalee Holloway (Netflix) - Nov. 4

What followed was years of unanswered questions, a missing teenager, and a mother's relentless fight for the truth. Now, over 20 years later, Natalee's mother, Beth, is ready to tell the complete story. With exclusive, unprecedented access to Beth and those who were with Natalee when she vanished, this three-part documentary series is the definitive account of a case that gripped a nation and never let go. It's a story of a mother who refused to stop searching, an investigation that spanned continents, and a daughter whose memory endures. This is Natalee's story, told at last in full.

Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook (Apple TV) - Nov. 6

Wolves Up Close With Bertie Gregory (National Geographic) - Nov. 6

But when she discovers that the town’s most feared man may actually be its most misunderstood, and the only person who can protect her from her dangerous ex-boyfriend, Maeve becomes entangled in Hunter’s world. As family secrets and a billion-dollar development deal threaten to unravel their growing connection, she must confront her past and decide how much she’s willing to risk for love.

When another attack splinters the small town of Pikeville, Charlotte – now a lawyer like her father – is the first witness on the scene. As the case unfolds and twists through painful memories and buried secrets, what emerges is not just a story of survival, but of enduring ties between a father and his daughters, and the complex bond between sisters.

After a reunion where the status of friendships and situationships remained ambiguous, the Charmers are determined to define their relationships and mend wounds. However, when true feelings bubble up and juicy rumors catch fire, the group seeks to unveil the truth – even if it costs them more than just friendships.

Three years into their jobs as response officers, Constables Grace Ellis, Tommy Foster, and Annie Conlon are operating at their limit, facing a new threat on the streets that the police can barely control. Meanwhile the murder trial of Gerry Cliff exposes a dangerous and long-buried secret that leads to chaos both inside the police, and across the criminal underworld. As they grapple with big decisions about their future, Grace, Tommy and Annie must find the courage to face the greatest threat they have ever encountered: the truth.

Each episode of the drama unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist, and the 12 days following the heist. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) who play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas (National Geographic) - Nov. 13

The documentary follows teams of National Geographic Explorers as they investigate our global Ocean, from seashore to seafloor and pole to pole. Combining cutting-edge technology with the knowledge of coastal communities, they chase the discoveries and solutions needed to protect our Oceans at a critical moment.

Homicide for the Holidays (Oxygen) - Nov. 14

The holidays are supposed to be the most wonderful time of the year. But for some families, cherished celebrations become the backdrop for unimaginable violence. Season six of Homicide For The Holidays brings a new batch of deadly deeds to the supposed jolliest time of the year as investigators pursue those responsible and seek justice for families shattered at a time meant for togetherness.

Diane Morgan returns as Philomena Cunk in a new series from Charlie Brooker. Billed as Cunk's most glamorous outing yet, she charts the history of cinema, from the invention of the camera and the New Wave filmmakers of the 1960s right up to the entrance of CGI and what the future of AI holds. Cunk will attempt to demystify it all while sitting in lumpy seats with stale popcorn, asking herself where did cinema come from? And why? What does it want? And why can’t it tell us?

Small Town Trouble: Texas (Bravo) - Nov. 18

Set in Boerne (pronounced "Bur-nee"), Texas, the series follows a charming yet unconventional group of wives, mothers and social insiders – Aaryn Williams, Alli McAnelly, Annari Uys, Gabby Hernandez Huffman, and Hailey Head, alongside their respective husbands – as conservative values of small-town life collide with forbidden attraction, messy friendships, and shocking   secrets. Here, perception is everything, temptation is everywhere, and the truth is never as buttoned-up as it looks.

The story of Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, two hyper-smart, ambitious young idealists who tried to remake the global financial system in the blink of an eye - before they were accused of stealing $8 billion and became Gen Z's own Bonnie & Clyde.

After years of nonstop touring, Nelly reflects on the physical toll it’s taking at this stage in his life, and an unexpected family loss reminds him what matters most. Between raising their son, honoring their village, and planning for their future, Nelly and Ashanti discover that belonging together isn’t about standing still; it’s about building a future on their own terms.

In the new two-hour special, viewers will dive headfirst into the bizarre true story that left an entire community searching for answers and asking one simple question: why?

As the survivors race to bury their sins before rescue arrives and an old flame roars back into town with plans of her own, turns out not every homecoming is a joyous one, and this one's going to sting.

Adapted from Tom Bradby's bestselling novel, Secret Service follows senior MI6 officer Kate Henderson (Gemma Arterton), whose covert investigation uncovers evidence that a high-ranking U.K. politician may be working as a Russian asset. With trust shattered and her career on the line, Kate must navigate the shifting sands of political loyalty, international threat, and personal sacrifice as she races to uncover their identity before it's too late.

The new comedy follows a team of dedicated archaeologists (and less-dedicated college students) who spend their summer working on a dig site in Greece. Their discovery of a rare artifact sends them on the adventure of a lifetime.

#778. EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

#777. An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De Miguel

Fans have been paying their respects to Tenerife's Jesus de Miguel following his death on Tuesday

As you arrive on the holiday island of Tenerife, there is a profound sense of grief, pain and disbelief at the death of footballer Jesus de Miguel.

The Canary island is in mourning for the Tenerife striker, who died from injuries sustained in a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday.

The 30-year-old had quickly established himself as a club favourite, scoring 11 goals in his first season as Tenerife were promoted to the second tier of Spanish football.

But now the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium has become a shrine to the player, with hundreds of people gathering throughout the past few days to lay flowers, light candles and pay their respects.

Bouquets, rosettes sent by clubs from across Spain, prayer cards, photographs, children's drawings and scarves have been laid around the grounds outside gate nine.

It is a deeply moving scene. Fans and residents stand in silence, taking in the tributes.

Many are visibly tearful as the scale of the loss begins to sink in at the very place the incident happened.

'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono

Among those paying their respects were Lisa and Lee, visiting Tenerife from Stoke-on-Trent.

They had arrived on holiday at the weekend and decided to attend Monday's match, hoping to experience Spanish football for the first time.

"We never expected something like this to happen," they told BBC Sport.

"We knew it was serious when the players surrounded him [De Miguel], but to see players crying and actually praying on the pitch was very emotional.

"When we found out the news the next day, it just really hit us."

The couple described the atmosphere inside the stadium as sombre and almost completely silent as spectators waited to understand what was happening.

"You always expect somebody to pull through," Lee said. "And then seeing the news the next day, it was just unbelievable."

They returned to the stadium on Wednesday to lay a Port Vale shirt among the tributes, wanting to show their support for the Tenerife community.

"Football has no colours," Lisa said. "If it was one of our players, we'd be heartbroken. They're part of your family."

For Carlos, a player with Tenerife's disability side Tenerife Foundation, the loss is particularly personal.

"Honestly, there are no words to describe him. He was incredible," Carlos said as he lay a flag on the ground.

He described De Miguel as a figure who had helped shape the club's recent history.

"He practically gave his heart and soul for the shirt. He's already a legend at the club because, after all, we were in a very difficult position a few years ago and he helped pull us out of it.

"Without him, I don't think we would be where we are today."

Carlos was at Monday's match and said he was left in shock by what unfolded.

"When I left the stadium I was trembling and I continued to feel that way for hours.

"Right now, we're incredibly hurt and very sad. I also want to send my support to his family, who I can only imagine must be absolutely devastated."

English fans in Tenerife pay tribute to De Miguel

The sense of loss has extended far beyond the stadium.

Poli Suarez, the Canary Islands' minister for education and sport, said Tenerife was in "complete mourning".

"Canarian sport has been left devastated," Suarez told BBC Sport. "The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken."

Suarez also stressed that the thoughts of everyone were with De Miguel's wife, daughter and wider family.

"They are the ones suffering most directly from this loss, just as the Tenerife supporters are suffering," he said.

The government has pledged its support to the club, players and supporters, with Suarez describing De Miguel as a footballer who had become part of the Canary Islands' sporting history.

"The loss of Jesus de Miguel is now part of our history," Suarez said.

"Not only because of the circumstances of his death, but also because of the affection he always showed towards our island and towards his club."

A further tribute is planned for Saturday at 18:00 GMT, with supporters encouraged to come together to honour his memory.

"It will be an opportunity to show our affection and emotion, and to demonstrate our solidarity with the family," Suarez said.

"We want to show all our affection for Jesus de Miguel."

#775. Why Matthew Stafford’s Wife Kelly Stafford Is Calling Out the NFL

Kelly Stafford, wife of Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, questioned the NFL's decision to schedule the Los Angeles team's bye week with only 10 days off, rather than the usual 11 to 14.

Kelly Stafford is throwing a flag on the NFL's schedule.

As the Los Angeles Rams continue to hit the field during the 2026 season, quarterback Matthew Stafford's wife sent a pointed message to the league about the team's calendar.

"Just curious to hear the thought process behind making the Rams the only team in the NFL without a true bye week," Kelly wrote on her Instagram Stories Nov. 3. "Because damn, after 18 years around this league, even I need a week off during the season… and I have never played a single snap."

The registered nurse—who shares 9-year-old twin girls Sawyer and Chandler, as well as daughters Hunter, 8, and Tyler, 6, with Matthew—may not be lacing up her cleats, but she knows when a time-out may be needed.

"I'm tired just watching from the stands," she continued. "Can't imagine how the guys feel."

Although teams generally have their bye weeks after a Sunday game and don't play again for 11 to 14 days, both the Rams and Green Bay Packers—who face off on the day before Thanksgiving (Nov. 25)—will return to the field after 10 days.

Other teams with a bye week at the same time, including the Cleveland Browns, New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks, will still take a full 14 days off.

E! News has reached out to the NFL for comment and has not yet heard back.

Not every schedule may be a touchdown, but the league does try its best to ensure each team has a restful week off, which is determined by the number of cross-country games scheduled, stadium conflicts and other operational obstacles.

"The scheduling teams aim to balance these operational elements while still trying to maximize fan viewership," the NFL Operations website explained. "The process is challenging, and there may be no such thing as a perfect schedule, but the schedule makers consistently try to provide the NFL's fans and broadcast partners with a compelling and entertaining slate of games week after week."

While Kelly is willing to call a foul on the Rams' calendar, she will always cheer on her husband, who has been her MVP since they married in 2015.

"He is the softest, most patient man," she told E! News in 2022. "My dad always said one of the most important relationships in life is a father-daughter relationship just because of the confidence your dad can give you."

"I am so grateful that I ended up with Matthew," she added, "because he sets such an incredible example as to the partner they should want to be with."

As the Staffords prepare for another week of football, keep reading for a closer look at their game-winning family moments.

On the field, Matthew Stafford is one of the best quarterbacks of the NFL. But when the football player comes home, he's simply dad.

During bye-week, Matthew and his wife Kelly Stafford treated their kids to a festive fall day near their home in Los Angeles.

"33 and grateful for the people that fill this home," Kelly wrote when celebrating her birthday. "Thankful for these girls' contagious smiles and for a husband who never fails to make me laugh."

"A pier breakfast, turned beach day, turned watching pro female surfing competition…" Kelly wrote on Instagram. "Pretty epic summer day with great 'aloha vibes.'"

After playing at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, Matthew was able to reunite with three of his daughters in a suite.

After cheering for Dad all day long, it's no surprise that Matthew's kids just want to snuggle after game day.

Whether they are at the stadium or going to school, Matthew's daughters love to wear the Rams' team colors.

When Matthew worked from home during COVID-19 shutdowns, his daughters quickly wore him out.

"My whole heart in one photo," Kelly wrote on Instagram when capturing her daughters snuggling by Matthew.

#774. Muriqi caps Fenerbahce comeback to make Liverpool pay for defensive lapses

Andoni Iraola arrived in Istanbul seeking improvement from Liverpool’s attack but departed with sudden cause for concern at the opposite end of the pitch. Fenerbahce ignited Dirk Kuyt’s interim spell with a tumultuous victory after Liverpool detonated their 100% Champions League record with several defensive lapses.

Liverpool’s second successive defeat left Iraola exasperated for entirely different reasons to Sunday’s loss to Arsenal. Blame was found only in the mirror this time around. It was so careless and so unnecessary.

The visitors led twice, through Trey Nyoni’s first senior goal and a header from substitute Alexander Isak, but Fenerbahce twice hit back quickly and snatched victory when Vedat Muriqi emerged as the strongest player from a pack of red shirts. Fenerbahce’s first goal came from a free-kick, their second from a corner and their third from a long throw-in.

“Cheap goals, messy goals,” as the Liverpool head coach put it. “We knew set pieces were one of the strengths of Fenerbahce. We have been dealing with them well, both this season and today, it has been something we have been working on since pre-season, but it cost us today. The last goal was maybe because they are strong and tall but the other two we have to control better.”

Ronald Araújo resting on the bench offers one explanation for Liverpool’s weak defensive display but does not cover every fault. The visitors enjoyed large spells of control and, despite an anonymous display from Bradley Barcola as the central striker, should never have given hope to an ageing, average Fenerbahce side packed with familiar names from the Premier League.

As expected, Turkish supporters tested the eardrums with incessant whistling whenever Liverpool took possession. They were a test for structural engineers too with their constant bouncing in the upper tier of the home end. Liverpool sought to dilute the atmosphere by controlling possession. Rio Ngumoha was prominent and N’Golo Kanté should have been booked for halting one promising run by leaping on the teenager’s back. Referee Clément Turpin was in a lenient mood with both sides.

Fenerbahce had struggled to hold up play in the Liverpool half or create a chance of note when Archie Brown exposed the visiting defence with a superb ball from left-back. The pass sailed over the struggling Kostas Tsimikas and was controlled well by Mason Greenwood, before he was pushed over by the Liverpool defender. Neither Turpin nor the video assistant referee deemed it a penalty kick.

The decibel levels cranked up and went even higher when Liverpool took the lead moments later. Ngumoha was heavily involved with a darting run and shot that was charged down into the path of Dominik Szoboszlai. Brown, under pressure from Virgil van Dijk, headed the midfielder’s cross clear but only as far as Nyoni. The young midfielder swept a low volley beyond Ederson with the aid of a slight deflection off Kojo Peprah Oppong. It was a memorable milestone in the continued rise of Nyoni; the first goal of his career at the highest level.

It was also the cue for Fenerbahce to rouse themselves. The hosts almost levelled straight from the restart when Brown’s low centre was turned against Alisson’s crossbar by Irfan Can Kahveci, who may have been ruled offside. They did not have to wait long for the equaliser. After Szoboszlai was penalised for a foul on Kanté, Greenwood’s resulting free-kick took a huge deflection off Jérémy Jacquet’s stomach and sailed past the wrongfooted Alisson. The Liverpool keeper did not hide his anger at Jacquet turning away from the free-kick and leaving a costly hole in the wall.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The second half mirrored the first with Liverpool in control until scoring and provoking a reaction from the Turkish side. Substitutes Cody Gakpo and Isak had only been on the pitch three minutes when they combined to restore the visitors’ advantage, the Swedish striker heading past Ederson from Gakpo’s left-wing cross.

But Fenerbahce again levelled swiftly when Kanté swept in a cross following a corner and Gakpo, attempting to head clear, glanced the ball away from Alisson’s grasp to give Brown a simple tap-in at the back post. “In the stadium it was almost impossible to communicate,” Iraola admitted. “It was difficult for me to give instructions and the communication must have been difficult between Cody and Ali.”

Worse was to come for Liverpool when Birmingham-born Brown looped a cross into the heart of Liverpool’s box. Muriqi, a second-half replacement for Romelu Lukaku, managed to hold off three Liverpool players – Jacquet, Alexis Mac Allister and Nyoni – and plant a header into the bottom corner. Iraola added: “It’s so frustrating because this is a difficult place to play and we were winning twice. We need to look at how we conceded the goals.”

#773. AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

A self-driving lab named AutoDNA can work out the constituent ‘letters’ in a snippet of DNA.Credit: Turtle Rock Scientific/Science Source/Science Photo Library

To say that someone has ‘good hands’ is high praise in a molecular biology laboratory, where researchers must deftly handle delicate glassware, pipette samples and more. But in an unusual genetics lab at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China, a team of robots driven by artificial intelligence is designing and doing experiments with no hands to speak of.

The facility, described today1 in Nature, is one of the latest steps towards ‘self-driving’ labs that are guided by AI, with minimal input from human scientists. With samples moved around by robotic arms, the Shanghai lab can operate more than 20 types of instrument, complete thousands of operations in a single project and do experiments that involve synthesizing and sequencing DNA, among other tasks.

An experiment is designed and executed from start to finish by a team of AI agents, following a simple prompt from a human operator. After that, human hands are needed only to refresh reagents and to service hardware.

The system, called AutoDNA, is remarkable both for its degree of autonomy and because it can readily incorporate a diverse range of lab equipment, says Milad Abolhasani, a chemical engineer at North Carolina State University in Raleigh. “The future of science is going to involve a lot of autonomous labs.”

Labs have long incorporated automation into their workflows, using machines to conduct specific aspects of experimental protocols, such as mixing and heating chemicals. Now, some researchers are hoping to harness increasingly sophisticated AI tools to create self-driving labs, in which an AI system designs and executes complex experiments, troubleshoots and tweaks protocols, and orchestrates activities across an entire lab that is chock-full of disparate equipment.

Designing such labs for molecular biology is challenging because of the field’s complex workflows, which require assorted equipment and high precision, says Haibo Chen, a computer scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and a co-author of the report. “In many existing systems, human experts are still required to configure the instruments,” he says. “AI is mostly added to handle just one part of the process.”

To create a more fully autonomous lab, Chen and his colleagues decided to construct it from the start with AI in mind, rather than adding AI capabilities to a pre-existing system.

The team tested AutoDNA by tasking it with a variety of projects, including detecting a cancer-linked mutation in a sample of DNA. In another experiment, the researchers asked the system to encode a message in DNA using its four nucleotide bases, abbreviated as A, C, G and T. They selected a popular quote, often misattributed to cosmologist Stephen Hawking: “Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change.”

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03552-8
